# LXR GC implementation roadmap

This roadmap tracks a greenfield port of LXR, described in Zhao, Blackburn, and McKinley's
[Low-Latency, High-Throughput Garbage Collection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.17175), to CoreCLR as a
standalone GC plus a set of generic runtime capabilities. The reference implementation is checked out at
`C:\github\lxr-reference`: [`mmtk-core`](https://github.com/wenyuzhao/mmtk-core) and
[`mmtk-openjdk`](https://github.com/wenyuzhao/mmtk-openjdk).

Two revisions are in scope as parity oracles. The oracle basis is the **binding-pinned pair** — the configuration
you get by checking out the binding and building it with no override: PLDI is binding `abbdd1d` (tag
`lxr-pldi-2022`) resolving core `df8d30a3`, and head is binding `0682434` (branch `lxr`) resolving core
`304ce69d`. This is deliberately *not* the core tag `4d4e516c` nor the core branch head `9625c174`: the binding
does not reference either, so building them requires a manual override, whereas the pinned pair is what a reader
of the paper reproduces without intervention. Since a multi-year port will be rebuilt by many future sessions,
reproducibility-without-intervention is the deciding property. The oracle is chosen **per mechanism** between the
two pairs and recorded in the P0.3 ledger with its reason.

The core tag and branch head were also built and measured, and are **behaviorally indistinguishable** from their
pinned counterparts: P0.1 found agreement in all 24 antlr/`-n 5` cells and identical pass sets across the DaCapo
matrix on both revisions. The choice above is therefore provenance, not behavior, and **every P0.1 number is
valid under either reading**. Those runs are retained as labelled secondary evidence and never share a table with
oracle numbers.

Beware the author date when reasoning about these revisions: `df8d30a3` was authored 2022-03-14 but committed
2022-04-10 after a rebase, so it is 9 commits **ahead** of `4d4e516c` despite appearing older; `9625c174` is 9
commits ahead of `304ce69d`. The PLDI nine are inert specifically under `--features lxr` — verified mechanically,
not just empirically: `014368ef` changes `LAZY_MU_REUSE_BLOCK_SWEEPING` from `true` to `cfg!(feature =
"lxr_lazy")`, which still evaluates true because `lxr` implies `lxr_lazy`, and `518e9bc2`/`c2657a63` gate
`max_copy` on `!cfg!(feature = "lxr")` so the else branch is byte-identical. "stw LXR" names the stop-the-world
variants, a different configuration. They nevertheless contain `rc_bits`, which makes `LOG_REF_COUNT_BITS`
feature-selectable (`lxr_rc_bits_{2,4,8}`) while preserving the default — so **RC width is a designed tunable,
default 2 bits with `MAX_REF_COUNT == 3`, and a port must parameterize it rather than hardcode it.** The head
nine are structural and not inert: the `plan/lxr` relocation trio, the concurrent-plan rework, the upstream
concurrent-marking interface switch, and bucket states, at 32 files and +1357/-1575.

`lxr-x/simplified` is explicitly **excluded**: it is a reduced fork (+1568/-2216 across 19 files versus
`lxr`) and measuring parity against it is a defect.

Full parity with the reference is a requirement, not an aspiration. Runtime changes are permitted and
preferred over GC-side approximation, but only as generic capability extensions for which LXR is the first
consumer rather than the definition.

## Operating rules

1. A step becomes `done` only in a separate verification pass after implementation, and only when the cited reference mechanism is present with the same ordering and transition provenance. Statuses are `planned`, `in_progress`, `done`, and `failed`; `in_progress` is set automatically when the Implement button spawns a child session, and is what prevents a second session being spawned for the same step.
2. Similar observable behavior is not acceptance evidence. Approximations, heuristics, and GC-side workarounds do not substitute for a reference mechanism; if a mechanism cannot be reproduced, the step fails rather than silently degrading.
3. Every mechanism declares which oracle it follows (`pldi-2022` = binding `abbdd1d` + core `df8d30a3`, or `lxr-head` = binding `0682434` + core `304ce69d`) and why; coupled mechanisms must share one oracle, because mixing revisions inside a coupled set produces a hybrid that is self-consistent nowhere. Where a claim was read from the core tag `4d4e516c` or branch head `9625c174` instead, the row says so — those builds are behaviorally indistinguishable from the pinned pairs but are not the declared basis.
4. Sweeping never parses objects. Nursery and mature reclamation read only the RC table, line/straddle metadata, and mark bits, walking at 8-byte granularity; any design that requires object-by-object heap parsing during a sweep is rejected.
5. Runtime changes follow R1-R5: generalize the mechanism not the client; zero measured cost when unused, by init-time selection rather than branching; additive and version-gated; independently defensible without LXR; performance evidence per change.
6. Every performance checkpoint compares the same binaries, machine state, workload input, duration, warmup, and run count across LXR, Workstation GC, and Server GC; pin DATAS, heap count/limit, concurrency, tiering, PGO, and ReadyToRun, then interleave collectors across invocations.
7. Report failures and excluded runs. Never select only successful LXR runs when a workload is flaky.
8. No code, status, or measurement is inherited from the abandoned `C:\github\runtimelab` prototype.
9. `src/plan/lxr/...` paths in the References fields below are **head-only**. At the PLDI oracle there is no LXR plan at all: LXR is a compile-time feature configuration of the Immix plan (`lxr = ["lxr_basic", "lxr_cm", "lxr_lazy", "lxr_evac"]` over `ix_ref_count`/`ix_concurrent_marking`), with `args.rs` at the crate root, block allocation under `policy/immix/`, concurrent marking in `util/cm.rs`, and the barrier in `mmtkFieldLoggingBarrier.cpp`. A missing PLDI path therefore never means a missing mechanism, and cross-revision comparison is mechanism-to-mechanism, never path-to-path. The compile-time-feature to runtime-`MMTK_PLAN` shift between the two oracles is itself a portability-relevant difference, since .NET selects a standalone GC at init time.
10. Never trust a reference build's exit code as evidence of what it built. `CompileThirdPartyHeap.gmk` expands `GC_FEATURES=--features $(MMTK_PLAN)` into `CARGO_BUILD_FEATURES = --features $(GC_FEATURES)`, so setting `MMTK_PLAN` emits `cargo build --features --features lxr`, which is silently ignored and yields **NoGC while appearing to be LXR**. Pass `GC_FEATURES=lxr,immix` with `MMTK_PLAN` unset — `immix` is required because the binding's `lib.rs` has no `lxr` case and the default `PlanSelector` is NoGC. Confirm the emitted `cargo build` line and the runtime banner (`barrier: FieldLoggingBarrier`, `ix_ref_count`, `lxr_*` features) before believing any measurement. Two further traps: the reference's own CI runs DaCapo at `-Xms500M -Xmx500M`, and the MarkCompact minheap table describes MarkCompact rather than LXR, so undersized heaps mimic total breakage; and under WSL `ulimit -c 0` does not stop the `core_pattern` capture pipe turning each SIGSEGV into a ~155 s stall that looks like a hang (`echo core > /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern`).
11. Classify every reference claim by how it was obtained: `[obs-oracle]` observed on a shipped pair, `[obs-override]` observed on a build that never shipped, `[read-only]` read but never executed. Order revisions with `git merge-base`, never by date — `df8d30a3` was rebased and its author date reverses the true topology. Scan **all** log directories before asserting a clean run; a release build with `cfg(debug_assertions)` checks compiled out carries the same corrupt state silently, so absence of a panic in release is not absence of a violation. A fix-shaped commit message does not imply the fix applies to your configuration: expand the feature gates before attributing a behavior change to a commit, and confirm with a differential run rather than inference.
12. Read the artifact, never a proxy for it. This failure mode has now recurred three times across P0.1 and P0.2: a TLS failure against the public PyPI CDN was generalized into "`pip install` is blocked" without ever running the command, which also produced "no PDF rasterizer exists" from the absence of standalone binaries when the `pymupdf` package renders in-process and made the step's own rendered-page check look impossible; a positional column index silently read `SATB%` in place of `!Lazy%` on rows with a different cell count; and Table 6's column membership was argued from prose when the page could simply be rendered and read. Never record a capability as unavailable without running it to completion and pasting the failure, never index a table column by position where row shapes vary, and prefer rendering a PDF page over trusting extracted text for anything structural. A claim about an artifact must cite the artifact — including one's own prior reports, which are artifacts too. P0.3 saw a correction issued against a child session's entirely accurate statement because the coordinator recalled which commit it had audited rather than re-reading its own transcript; the child settled it by fingerprinting the two trees (`redirectBlock=0` at `080ae02120b`, `1` at `5712425e3ed`). Check your own record before contradicting someone about what is in it, or the discipline is only ever pointed outward.
13. Absence of a check is not evidence of an invariant. The two oracles do not carry the same assertions: at PLDI the RC invariant is asserted in the write barrier slow path (`src/plan/barriers.rs:315-319`, condition at `:316`, gated `cfg(any(feature = "sanity", debug_assertions))`), while at `304ce69d` no barrier-side check exists and the only `zero rc count` assertion lives in `src/util/sanity/sanity_checker.rs:311-316` (condition at `:312`) behind `cfg(feature = "sanity")` — a non-default feature the build recipe never enabled. Both of those spans were first cited here one line off, at `:317` and `:313`, because grepping for the message literal lands on the format-string line rather than the condition; cite multi-line assertion macros as a span and name the condition line. So "HEAD never trips it" recorded an uncompiled check as a passing one, and validate-against-lxr-head must first re-instate the invariant at the validating revision before a clean run means anything. Before citing a clean run as validation, confirm the check exists and was compiled into the binary that produced it.
14. Cite reference locations at the declared oracle revision, never from the checkout. `C:\github\lxr-reference/mmtk-core` is checked out at the named `9625c174`, not at the declared oracle `304ce69d`, and the two differ in tree shape: `304ce69d` has a flat 9-file `src/plan/lxr/` with `cm.rs`, `gc_work.rs` and `remset.rs`, while `9625c174` has 13 files with a `gc_work/` subdirectory plus `block_allocation.rs`. A path read from the working tree can therefore name a file that does not exist at the oracle. All four revisions exist as objects in that clone, so cite with `git show <rev>:<path>` in `<rev>:<path>` form. A bare `:NNN` shorthand is only as good as the last full path before it: P0.3 wrote `plan/lxr/global.rs:707`/`:708` without the `src/` prefix, so the extractor bound `:708` to the preceding full path instead — which resolved, to a `cfg(feature = "vo_bit")` line. Shorthand that silently rebinds still resolves, so keep a full path with every citation that starts a new file.
15. A citation is not evidence unless the cited code is compiled in the configuration under discussion. Locating text at a line proves only that the text is there. P0.3 cited `plan/immix/global.rs:532-534` and `plan/lxr/global.rs:377-379` as both oracles ignoring `System.gc()`; both are `cfg(feature = "nogc_no_zeroing")`, a feature in neither oracle's default set and never enabled by the build recipe, so neither line is compiled. The live paths are `memory_manager.rs:686` to `mmtk.rs:436` to `util/heap/gc_trigger.rs:143` at HEAD, which sets the flag and requests the collection, and at PLDI the trait default `plan/global.rs:590-598`, whose body is entirely commented out. Dead code that reads correctly is the sharpest form of this trap, and a mechanical citation checker cannot catch it because the text resolves. Establish that a cited line is reachable in the built configuration before treating it as behavior, and state the configuration alongside the citation.
16. A verification tool must audit the artifact it ships with, and must be run against committed content. `scripts/verify-ledger.sh:18` defaulted its document root to an absolute path inside one worktree, so running the committed script from a clean `git archive` extract silently audited a different, mid-edit checkout — reporting a failure the committed tree did not have, and equally able to report a pass it had not earned. P9.1 is specified to lean on this gate, so an auditor running it from a fresh clone would either fail on an absent path or attest to a tree they are not looking at. Derive default inputs from `${BASH_SOURCE[0]}` so a script always checks the tree it ships in, let an explicit argument override, and derive expected counts from the document instead of repeating a literal at several assertion sites. Two corollaries: run the gate on extracted committed content rather than a working tree before treating its exit code as evidence, and remember that an `i/lf` script checked out `w/crlf` cannot be executed by bash at all, so a pass obtained from a converted copy attests to the copy rather than to the artifact.
17. A control that has not been shown to fire is indistinguishable from an absent one. P0.3 had to reject three controls that reported success while testing nothing: a reach counter whose abort threshold was an order of magnitude too high; a gate control that deleted row `E03`, which this ledger does not contain, so its `sed` matched nothing; and a gate control that perturbed its own input tree in place and then re-ran the gate on the tree it had just broken. This is the tooling-side twin of rule 13 — absence of a failure signal is evidence only once that signal has been demonstrated. Every check that gates a claim ships with a demonstration that it fails when the thing it checks is broken: perturb a throwaway copy rather than the input, assert the perturbation actually applied before trusting either verdict, and require the pair (clean pass, perturbed fail) rather than the pass alone. A control must also fire *reliably*, and P0.4 supplied the counter-example: its barrier-scale control asserted that a ~2% injected slowdown was resolved, then reached that target at n=8, at n=15, and not at all across three runs of the same binary on the same host, with the injected effect once measuring `0.9906` against a null replicate of `0.9912`. Direct probing outside the harness returned ratios of `1.0221`, `0.9649` and `0.9922` — a 2% signal under a ±3% spread, with the sign flipping — so the flake was the machine, not the harness. Gating a verdict on a signal below the measurement floor makes the outcome track ambient load, which is as useless as a control that never fires and worse in one respect: it teaches the next reader that the route to green is to rerun or loosen the threshold, which is choosing the acceptance criterion from the result. Split such a control rather than tuning it — assert on a magnitude the environment cannot miss (`0.8122 [0.8023, 0.8220]` for a ~16.7% injection), pair it with a null replicate so an over-confident estimator cannot pass by manufacturing an effect (`1.0085 [0.9978, 1.0195]`), and keep publishing the marginal measurement unasserted so the information survives without the flake. Name the blind band this leaves: between the asserted coarse magnitude and the unasserted fine one, a resolution regression fails nothing, so consider a deliberately generous bound on the fine arm chosen the same way the coarse one was.
18. Verify a hash, then push that hash. Worktrees share branch refs, so `git push origin <branch>` resolves the ref at push time rather than at verification time. P0.3 was audited at `0ab50bf3d04` and PR #3 was opened on `814a1967985`, because the child session committed in the seconds between the `git archive` and the push — putting a commit into a pull request that the verification statement in its body did not cover. The cost of a stale read is not the wasted time, it is the false attestation. This is also the only failure this project has hit that no single participant could see: every earlier instance was a claim about the wrong artifact inside one process, whereas here one session moved a shared ref between another session's two reads. Prefer the form that is correct by construction over the one that is correct by inspection — `git push origin <sha>:refs/heads/<branch>` makes the verified object and the pushed object the same by definition, and if the ref has moved since, it pushes less than the branch or is rejected outright, never more and never something unread. Re-reading the remote head afterwards is the weaker fallback because it detects the problem instead of preventing it. Name the verified hash in the PR body so a later reader can tell what the claim covers, and prefer attestations that can be re-checked over ones that must be trusted: a hash in the body can be compared against the head by anyone at any time, whereas a ref-relative phrase such as "this branch's head" reads as true at every future moment and silently covers whatever is there then. That was the form this rule's own pull request took on the first attempt, written an hour after the rule. The same applies in reverse when auditing a child: read its tip before grepping, since a correction may already be committed above the commit in hand.

19. A squash merge does not preserve the commit you verified, so the verification has to be repeated against what actually landed. PR #3 was verified and attested at `814a1967985`, but merging squashed it into `8a63e85178b`, a commit with a single parent whose ancestry does not contain the verified hash at all. `git merge-base --is-ancestor 814a1967985 origin/main` answers no. The tree happened to be byte-identical, but that is a fact to be checked rather than assumed, and once the branch is deleted the attested object may become unreachable entirely — leaving a pull request body naming a hash that no longer exists in the repository, which is an attestation a later reader cannot check against anything. This is the mirror image of rule 18: there the ref moved under a fixed verification, here the verification stayed fixed while the object it named was replaced. Treat the merge commit, not the branch tip, as the artifact a step's closure evidence refers to; re-run the gate against an extract of the merge commit and record that hash in the roadmap. A step is not done because its pull request is merged, it is done because the merged artifact was shown to pass.

20. Re-read the state you are gated on before reporting that you are still blocked on it. P0.3 sat unmarked for two hours after PR #3 merged because the gate was "waiting on the merge" and nothing prompted a re-read; the answer to "why is this not done" was that it was done and had not been looked at. This is rule 12 in its laziest form — the artifact was one command away and the stale proxy was my own last report. A blocked item carries an obligation to re-check its unblocking condition, not merely to wait for someone to announce it.

21. A claim about code you cannot read is a guess, and a moral drawn from a fabricated failure is worse than no moral. The P0.4 child reported that a benchmark file emitted without the `checkpoints` wrapper "parses without error and contributes nothing to the board — the quietest possible failure", and drew from it the lesson that one must read the artifact rather than a description of it. The lesson is right; the evidence for it was invented. The canvas is not committed on `main` and was absent from that worktree, so the claim was reasoning about unreadable code, and it is false: `store.mjs` merged such a file through `document.checkpoints ?? [document]`, so the flattened record *did* load and *did* chart. Writing that exact file and reading it back through the running canvas settled it in one command. The fix shipped alongside the claim was still correct, because the wrapper is the documented shape — but a correct fix resting on a mechanism that does not exist teaches the next reader to defend against the wrong thing, and an invented failure mode is not made harmless by an accurate remedy. The check paid for itself twice: that same tolerant fallback turned a file with a mistyped key into a checkpoint with no `date`, whereupon the sort comparator threw on `left.date.localeCompare` and **one malformed agent-produced file blanked the entire board**, phases and steps included — a real defect, in my own code, found only by testing someone else's wrong claim instead of accepting it. Files arriving from agents will be malformed sometimes, so per-file isolation, a required `schemaVersion`, and a named reason for every ignored file are now part of the contract rather than politeness. Verifying a claim you expect to confirm is how you find the bug that neither of you was looking for. Two refinements came back from the child session that are sharper than the correction itself, and both are the durable part. First, **the invented failure was milder than the truth**: "silently dropped" is the safer of the two behaviours, so the argument for the fix ran backwards — the real defect was that an unvalidated record was *charted as a real measurement*, and a fabricated failure mode understating severity is more dangerous than one overstating it, because it sets the remedy's urgency too low. Second, **a test of your own producer can only ever confirm your own producer.** The unit test asserting the flattened shape is rejected passed the entire time the claim was false, and could not have caught it: it exercised the emitter, while the claim was about a consumer outside the repository. Contract claims need the real consumer in the loop — rendering the file is what settled it. Where a consumer cannot be run, the honest form is "the documented shape is X, so emit X", which needs no behavioural claim at all.

22. Correct a false claim in place rather than rewriting it away, and re-verify at the corrected hash. The claim in rule 21 was already committed, pushed and cited in PR #4's body when it was found to be false. Deleting the sentence would have left a document that was correct and a history that silently disagreed with the numbers a reader had already seen; instead the section now states what it claimed, that the claim was false, and what the artifact actually does. The mechanical obligations that follow are easy to skip once the prose is fixed: the tip moved to `f5f1c6ed8b3`, so the gate was re-run from a fresh extract of *that* commit (`PASS (87 checks)`), the branch was pushed by hash rather than by ref, and the pull request body — which named the old hash in an attestation sentence — was rewritten to name the new one. An attestation naming a superseded hash is worse than none, because it reads as verified while covering a tree that no longer exists at that ref. Fixing the artifact and leaving the attestation stale converts a caught error into an uncaught one.

23. A search that cannot match is indistinguishable from an absence, and reports as one. Rule 15 says a hit may be meaningless because the text is not compiled; this is its inverse and it is the more dangerous half, because a miss produces no artifact to inspect and closes the question instead of opening it. Three instances in this effort, all different mechanisms and all reading as clean negatives: the P0.3 `zero rc count` spans were recorded a line off because grepping a message literal lands on the format-string line rather than the condition, so the probe hit the wrong thing while appearing to hit the right one; a HEAD comparison was believed to have run when its assertion sat behind a non-default `sanity` feature and was compiled out, so the search for failures returned nothing because nothing could fail; and a grep of the pushed commit messages for a claim known to be there returned empty because pipe-separated alternatives were passed to PowerShell's `-SimpleMatch`, which searches for the literal string `a|b|c` and can never match. That last one nearly became an accusation that a correct report was itself unverified — a null result laundering into a positive claim about someone else's work. Before believing a negative, prove the probe can fire: run it against a case known to match, or invert it and confirm the hit you expect. This is what control `[E]` does for the verification gate, asserting that a section emptied of checks is detected rather than silently passing, and it is the same obligation applied to the searches used to build the argument in the first place.

24. A coordinator that commits onto a child's branch has invalidated the child's picture of its own tree, and owes it the notice it would demand in return. The P0.4 child apologised for landing `5160725dcdd` while a fresh-extract verification of `d78a43684e3` was in flight — correctly, since "harmless this time" is a property of the delta and not of the practice. Within the hour the coordinator did the same thing to it in the opposite direction, committing the §10 correction `f5f1c6ed8b3` onto `kkokosa-p0-4-benchmark-harness` from a different worktree, after having raised the very complaint. The child's next report named `5160725dcdd` as its tip and was wrong about its own branch, and no amount of care on its side could have prevented that. The rule that follows is symmetric with rule 20: whoever moves a ref tells whoever is reading it, before the next exchange rather than after. Two details worth keeping because they cut in opposite directions. The child attributed a branch *rename* to the same interference; the reflog shows it renamed `kkokosa-crispy-robot` to `kkokosa-p0-4-benchmark-harness` itself at 09:56:24, nearly three hours before its own first commit — so it apologised for the right failure while misattributing half its cause, which is rule 23 again, a confident account of state nobody had re-read. And it doubted the coordinator's "our trees agree" and checked rather than deferring, which is the behaviour worth having: it was wrong that time, and being willing to be wrong that way is what makes its agreement worth anything.

25. A gate that audits an artifact against itself cannot catch the artifact lying about the code, and every capability a document claims is the cheapest possible assertion. `P0.4-harness.md` states at line 87 that P0.4 "implements the mechanism and a `calibrate` mode that bisects for a scenario's minimum viable heap", and repeats at line 881 that "the `calibrate` mechanism ships". Neither is true: `RunnerOptions.cs:71` accepts `matrix`, `controls`, `conformance` and `hosts`, and no `Calibrate` symbol exists anywhere in the harness. That document passed a gate run five ways at three different hashes, from clean `git archive` extracts, with the check count deliberately investigated when it moved between 71 and 87 — and none of it could ever have caught this, because every check compared the document to itself or to the results beside it. Grepping the source for the verb the document claims to ship is one line and would have failed instantly; the gate contains twenty-three lines mentioning `scenario` and **zero** mentioning `heap` or `calibrat`. The general form is that self-consistency is not correspondence, and the checks worth adding are the ones that cross the boundary between the document and the thing it describes. The same blindness hid a second defect of a different kind: `MatrixRunner.Run` calls `MatrixPlanner.Expand` with seven arguments, omitting the optional eighth `heapLimitForScenario`, so `MatrixCell.HeapLimitMb` is unconditionally `null`, the guard at `MatrixRunner.cs:242` never fires, and `System.GC.HeapHardLimit` is never set — while `:249` still passes `--heap-factor` through to the worker and `RunResult.cs:257` still publishes it. Running the paper's `{1.3, 2.0, 6.0}` would therefore have emitted three identically-configured unpinned runs under three different heap labels. It published nothing false only because nothing exercised it: all 528 `heapFactor` fields across the 474 preserved P0.4 result files are `null`, against 528 non-null `scenario` fields by the same method, so the trap was armed and never sprung. A latent fabrication mechanism is not a smaller bug than a realised one; it is the same bug waiting for its first user, and its first user was the step that had to trust it.

26. Prefer a probe that shows its evidence to one that returns a verdict, because a verdict hides its own misfires. Checking that claim about `heapFactor` began with `"heapFactor"\s*:\s*(?!null)`, intended to find non-null values and expected to return nothing. It returned five hundred and twenty-eight matches — every one of them a line reading `"heapFactor": null`, the exact text the lookahead was written to exclude. The cause is ordinary regex backtracking: `\s*` matches zero characters, the lookahead is then evaluated against ` null` rather than `null`, and it succeeds. Had that probe been written to emit a count or a boolean, it would have reported non-null heap factors in the preserved evidence — a fabricated defect in a merged artifact, produced by a search that ran cleanly and was read too quickly. It was caught for one reason only: `Select-String` prints the matched line, and the matched lines visibly said `null`. This is the counterpart to rule 23 rather than a repeat of it — 23 is a probe that cannot fire reading as an absence, this is a probe that fires wrongly reading as a finding — and the same discipline answers both: state what the probe should return before running it, make it print what it matched, and replace a clever exclusion with two counts and a subtraction whenever the question is "are there any". The rewritten check counted all occurrences and null occurrences separately and ran the identical method against a field known to be populated, which is what turned an assertion into a measurement. The habit paid again twice in one session: a preservation filter whose `-and`/`-ne` precedence was wrong copied 143 files where roughly 1,600 were expected, caught only because the count was compared against a prior inventory rather than accepted; and a `Select-String -Pattern 'FAIL'` over a passing test run reported one hit, which was the summary line `0 failed`, because PowerShell's matching is case-insensitive by default. Neither would have surfaced from a green tick.

27. A successful write is not a successful publish; confirm your own content reached the reader. The P0.5 roadmap entry was written with `Evidence`, `Corrections carried` and `Open` fields, the file saved correctly, the markdown was valid, the board reloaded, and the canvas reported `problems: 0` — while all three fields were discarded in silence. `parseRoadmap` called `parseField` once per known field name and simply never looked for anything else, so an unrecognised `- **Name:** value` line had no reader and produced no complaint. This was found only by querying the parsed state for text that had just been authored, which is a cheap habit and the only thing that distinguishes "written" from "published". It is the same failure the project already legislated against for agent-supplied benchmark files, where every ignored file must carry a named reason, and it had been sitting in the sibling code path the whole time — a contract enforced on other people's inputs and not on one's own. The parser now reads every field generically, promotes the known ones, and carries unknown ones through to the modal as labelled blocks, so a future step inventing a field gets it displayed rather than deleted; the fix was verified in both directions through a real click on a real card, one step showing its evidence and its two extra blocks and another correctly hiding an absent evidence block. The general rule is that a pipeline with a silent drop in the middle looks identical to one with nothing to carry, and the author is the only person positioned to notice the difference.

28. A gate that verifies data against data does not verify prose against data, and the sentence is where the claim actually lives. `P0.5-baselines.md:543` states that all four throughput ratios in the s2/s3 comparison drift by less than the 8.35% floor; `raw/arm-ratio-stability-s2-vs-s3.csv` — committed in the same directory, in the same commit — puts `long-lived-cache` at **8.744%**. It is three of four. The gate passed thirty checks over that sentence, and could not have done otherwise: it re-derives the arm-ratio CSV with `compare-arm-ratios.py`, compares committed rows to recomputed rows, and asserts the row *count* with `wc -l`, so the data was checked exhaustively and the paragraph describing it was never read. This is rule 25's twin — 25 is the artifact lying about the code, this is the artifact lying about its own data — and it is more insidious, because the false sentence and the refuting number ship in the same commit and neither is wrong in isolation. It propagated: the child asserted it to the coordinator, the coordinator repeated it verbatim in the PR body posted under the user's account and again in this roadmap, and it survived three readings by two parties because everyone who saw the number was reading a different artifact from everyone who saw the sentence. The conclusion it decorated was never in danger — `long-lived-cache`'s ratio is still 3.3× more stable than its absolute, and all four rows carry `ratioMoreStableThanAbsolute = true` — which is the trap: a false sentence attached to a true finding attracts no scrutiny at all. Two practices follow. Every quantified prose claim — "all N", "N of M", any comparison against a threshold — is a check the gate can run against the CSV, and should. And a table nobody can regenerate is one nobody can audit: §6.4 ships no generator, so recomputing it required reverse-engineering that its cells partition by `runId` and not by the `mode` field, and partitioning the obvious way returns 53 cells at 1.792% against a published 59 at 1.60% — a discrepancy that reads exactly like a defect and is not one. Publish the generator alongside the table, or the next reader's correct method is indistinguishable from their mistake.

29. A measurement rule that names one step will be orphaned by the step that follows it; project-wide constraints belong in the rules, not in a carry-forward. P0.5 concluded that LXR must be compared against a baseline arm measured in the same session, and expressed it as "P0.6 onward must" — in a document with no P0.6, whose next step was P1.1, a runtime-enablement step that measures nothing. The coordinator copied that phrasing into this roadmap and into the pull request body without checking that the addressee existed, which is rule 23's shape applied to a cross-reference rather than to code: a confident statement about a thing nobody had looked up. Two rules follow, and both are now recorded here rather than in a step. **First, every LXR benchmark carries its own baseline arm from the same session.** Between two sessions on this host the same throughput cell moved by a median of 12.15% and a maximum of 28.49%, while the within-session `srv`/`wks` ratio drifted 7.28% median against 19.06% for the corresponding absolutes — quoting the 28% alone against those medians compares a worst case with two typical cases, which is the kind of mismatch this project exists to catch. A baseline table read months later and compared against a fresh LXR number is not evidence. **Second, the shared heap limit moves when LXR joins.** The arithmetic is derived, stated and gated in `P0.5-baselines.md` §5.1, and is deliberately *not* restated here beyond the load-bearing fact that `srv` binds every calibrated row, so every absolute limit P0.5 publishes is a function of the Server arm's minimum alone. Adding a third collector makes the shared minimum `max(wks, srv, lxr)`, so for any scenario where LXR needs more than `srv` the cell's absolute limit rises and both existing arms land somewhere else on their own heap-size curves. That is not drift and the ratio rule does not repair it; it means P0.5's absolute tables cannot serve as a comparison arm across the LXR boundary for any cell whose limit moves, and the first step to measure LXR must recalibrate the shared minimum with LXR included and re-measure all three arms at the new limits — including when LXR's minimum turns out *lower* than Server's everywhere, since that negative result also has to be established by a run rather than assumed. The pointer rather than a copy is deliberate and was earned: this rule previously carried its own transcription of the Workstation and Server ranges, the document carried the same numbers in §5.1, **and both were false in the same way** — Workstation's minimum was given as a flat 4 MiB against a Server range of 35–43, which is true of exactly the four rows where Workstation sits at 4 and false of the ten-row matrix, where Workstation ranges over 4, 11, 19, 35 and 99 against Server's 35 to 139. Correcting the copy on this board left the copy in the document still false. A fact worth stating twice is a fact that will be wrong in one place and right in the other, and the reader has no way to tell which. The nominal label already describes the two existing arms differently — at nominal 1.3x, `srv` sits at 1.30–1.31x of its own minimum while `wks` sits at 1.83–14.00x, and at 6.0x `wks` reaches 64.5x — and since the paper's own throughput result inverts with heap generosity at 0.97, 0.96 and 1.01, this is a confound in precisely the dimension the port is judged on.

30. Two measurements that agree are corroboration only if they could have disagreed; methods sharing a degenerate failure mode agree perfectly and read as confirmation. Verifying the child's claim that its scripts are committed LF-only, a PowerShell probe counted carriage returns and reported non-zero for all fourteen. The obvious explanation was PowerShell's own CRLF conversion, so the check was re-run through bash on the raw blob — and returned *exactly the same fourteen numbers*, which was taken as evidence that the first result stood and the scripts were CRLF. Both were wrong. The bash script had itself been written with CRLF line endings, so `$'\r'` was mangled into a pattern that matched every line, and `grep -c` returned the line count; the PowerShell form had materialized the blob as text, introducing the very CRs it then counted, which also equals the line count. Two independent routes to the same wrong answer, agreeing to the digit. The tell was there to be read and was not: every file's "CR count" equalled its line count exactly, a coincidence across fourteen files of differing size that no real measurement produces. What settled it was refusing to compare the two suspect methods against each other and instead comparing each against something with a known answer — `od -c` on the raw bytes showing `\n`, git's own `git ls-files --eol` reporting `i/lf w/lf` for all fourteen, `tr -cd '\r' | wc -c` returning zero, and a three-line all-LF control file that the buggy pattern duly reported as containing three CRs. The claim under test had been true from the start; the verification invented the defect. So when two methods agree, ask what they share before treating it as independent confirmation, check the suspicious number against a quantity it should *not* equal, and run the method itself against an input whose answer is already known — the same control-input discipline the gate-of-the-gate applies to gates, turned on one's own probes. Agreement is the weakest evidence available when both parties can be wrong the same way.

31. Name the command that verifies an artifact, because the conventional one may pass without running anything. The P0.4 harness deliberately carries no `PackageReference` — so that it restores with no feed and runs on CoreRun, where there is no package resolution — which makes `Lxr.Harness.Tests` an `OutputType=Exe` assertion runner with no test adapter. `dotnet test` against it **exits 0 having run nothing**: five lines of restore output, no warning, no `0 tests`, no indication of any kind that no test executed. Running the assembly directly prints `58 passed, 0 failed`. Both were reproduced against the repository SDK rather than reasoned about, and the two transcripts are indistinguishable to anyone reading an exit code. This is rule 23's shape — a probe that cannot fire, reading as a pass — but it earns its own entry because it is not a mistake anyone made, it is a permanent property of a correct design decision, and it sits directly under the sentence "58 harness unit tests pass" in a pull request body published under the user's account. A reviewer doing exactly the right thing, reaching for the standard command to check a stated result, would have been told the result was confirmed. The rule generalises past this harness: whenever the natural verification command is not the correct one, the artifact must say so at the point it makes the claim, because a claim and its verification method are one statement and publishing the first without the second invites a false confirmation. The trap also inverts and both directions must be checked — `dotnet test` here fails on an SDK that cannot target the harness's framework, which looks like a broken test suite and is not, so the same paragraph must name the SDK the command needs.

32. A quantified claim inherits the population that was in view when it was written, silently, and a claim that is true of a subset is not a weaker error than one that is false — it is a harder one, because every number in it checks out. Three instances landed in a single step, in three different sections, written by two different parties. §6.4's CV table partitions its cells by `runId`; partitioning the obvious way, by the `mode` field, returns 53 cells at 1.792% against a published 59 at 1.60%, and the coordinator nearly reported that as a defect. §6.5's medians were re-derived by the implementer's own checker over the *disagreeing* subset and came back 17.94% and 18.16% against a published 14.48% and 16.19% — two more false claims, nearly reported, both published figures correct and the derivation wrong. And §5.1 shipped "Workstation never binds anywhere in this matrix. Its minimum is 4 MiB where Server needs 35–43", whose first sentence holds at 30 of 30 and whose second is false of the matrix: `wks` minima take five distinct values — 4, 11, 19, 35, 99 — and `srv` spans 35 to 139. Over the four rows where `wks` is exactly 4, `srv` is exactly {35, 43}. The sentence is a true statement about four rows wearing the grammar of a statement about ten. The coordinator committed the same error in the same exchange from the other direction, calling `large-object-pressure` "the one row that fails exact multiplication" when all ten fail it — a comparison tolerance had quietly defined a population of one and the conclusion was reported as though it described the matrix, so a universal was published as a singleton. What catches this is never the number, which is correct; it is a second sentence that cannot coexist with the first, and §5.1 supplied one twenty-one lines later by putting `wks` at 99. Two defences, both cheap. Every quantified claim names its population in the sentence — "across all 16 cells", "in 30 of 30 rows", "over the four scenarios where" — so that the subset reading and the whole-population reading stop being equally grammatical. And a checker that derives an expected value must derive it over a population it names and print that population beside the result, because a checker silently choosing the wrong subset agrees with wrong prose enthusiastically and reports a pass. Note what all four instances have in common: each decorated a conclusion that was true and survived the correction intact, which is precisely why nobody looked. A fourth variant arrived later in the same step and is worth separating, because it is the partition rather than the population that slips: a correction offered to this coordinator decomposed eighteen changed harness files as "5 new, 12 modified, 1 `.csproj`", which totals correctly while moving the project file out of the modified bucket it belongs to — the true split is 5 added and 13 modified, the `.csproj` being one of the thirteen. The conclusion resting on it was right and useful, that one modified file is the test program itself so 58 assertions guard 16 product sources rather than 18. **A correct total is not evidence of a correct partition**, and a decomposition that sums to the right answer is the easiest kind to accept without checking — especially when it arrives as someone else's correction of you, which is the one direction in which scrutiny is hardest to sustain. — **It recurred, in the same document, by the same column, and this time it went all the way to a composed board edit.** Verifying the implementer's falsification of §6.3's superlative I partitioned the latency phase by `mode` rather than `runId` — the identical substitution this rule already records me *nearly* reporting against §6.4's CV table — and produced a complete, self-consistent, wrong table: `aspnet-request-load` at **226.513 ms** against the true **451.592**, a 1.99x error, with a band split of **4 too close / 4 inside / 1 too far** against the correct **3 / 3 / 3**, and a cell-level closest approach of 1.50x against the true 2.98x. I was drafting a message calling the implementer's 3/3/3 wrong. On the correct discriminator every one of its ten figures reproduces to the digit — 451.592, 8.6x, 19.5x, 49.6x, 130x, 437x, 806x, 1604x, 1858x, 3105x, and 283.878 against 95.284. **The cross-tab is the whole story:** `runId=...latency` × `mode=latency` is 300 rows, `runId=...throughput` × `mode=throughput` is 265 — and `runId=...throughput` × `mode=latency` is **30**, exactly `aspnet-request-load`'s six cells × five invocations. `mode` is a *scenario's shape*, not a *phase*, and it takes the phases' own vocabulary as its values, which makes it the most confusable column in the file. **Rule 32's stated defence does not reach this.** I did name the population — “latency-phase” — and the name was right while the column was wrong; naming protects against a silent subset, not against believing the wrong field encodes the one you named. Two defences do reach it. First, rule 83 already specified it and I had read it: *all four consumers join on `runId`*, “unsafe the moment a P0.6 tool joins on `mode`” — so **join on the key the artifact's own consumers join on**, which is a grep rather than a judgement, and `rederive-statistics.py:134`'s `phase_of(row["runId"])` is the grep. Second, the data said so: every `aspnet` cell held **ten** values in two clean clusters — five near 1 ms, five near 400–700 ms — with `arrivalRatePerSecond` reading **1000** beside **8000** in the next column along. **A cell whose values are bimodal by 300x is not one population, and that is checkable without knowing which column is right.** The rule fired correctly and I was the one who walked past it, two hours after reading rule 84 — which cites `phase_of(row["runId"])` in its own text — in full. **The implementer then generalised the defect past my own account of it, and the generalisation is exact — verified here independently from the s2 CSV.** I had concluded the defences were *join on the key the consumers join on* and *notice the bimodality*. Both hold, and both are things I failed to do. But neither explains why the warning already on this board stopped me at “nearly” the first time and did not stop me at all the second, and the answer is that **the substitution is asymmetric, so the defence I actually learned the first time is structurally incapable of firing the second.** `mode` and `runId` agree in **565** of s2's 595 valid rows and diverge in **30**, and all 30 are `aspnet-request-load` — the one scenario driven open-loop in *both* phases. On the **throughput** side those rows are labelled `mode=latency`, so filtering by `mode` drops aspnet's six cells out of the population entirely: **53 cells against 59**, and the six missing are exactly `aspnet-request-load`×{`wks`,`srv`}×{1.3, 2.0, 6.0}. **A cell count detects that, and a cell count is what stopped me.** On the **latency** side the same six cells are present under *both* keys — the 30 stray rows do not create cells, they **merge into six that already exist**, taking the row count from 300 to 330 while the cell count stays **60 either way**, both set-differences empty. Nothing about the population's size or membership changes; only the statistic moves, median CV **11.670% to 12.343%**. **So the general form is about detectability rather than about columns: a substitution that changes set membership is caught by cardinality, and one that changes only multiplicity inside existing members is invisible to it.** The same wrong key does both, in two sections of one document, and the section where counting works is the one that teaches the reader to count. **A defence learned from the instance where it fires is not thereby a defence — it can be a detector calibrated on the only case it can see**, which is rule 74's shape moved from an instrument's controls to a reader's habits. What survives both sections is the pair that does not depend on the perturbation being visible: check which column the producing code joins on, and treat a cell whose values fall in two clusters 300x apart as more than one population.

33. A count stated as a literal beside a count that is computed will diverge, and the artifact will keep printing both. `verify-gate-of-the-gate.sh` closes by printing `RESULT: PASS (%d of %d cases behaved as required)` from live counters and then, on the very next line, the fixed string "The gate passed a clean extract, refused an empty one, and failed five single perturbations." At the commit where that sentence was written it was true. Two commits later the script ran ten cases: two clean extracts, one refusal, and **seven** perturbations — and it reported "10 of 10" and "five" in adjacent lines of the same output, one derived and one asserted, with nothing to reconcile them. The location is what makes it worth a rule: this is the control script, the artifact whose entire purpose is to prove the gate detects claims that data does not support, and it was making one. A hardcoded number is a second place for a fact to live, and the second place is never updated by the change that invalidates it — the same reason the prose checkers in this step compute every expected value at run time rather than storing it, applied to output rather than to input. Either derive the summary from the same counters that produced the verdict, or state no numbers in it at all; prose that restates a computed result in words is not documentation, it is an unversioned copy. The follow-up made the case better than the original did. Asked to derive the number or drop it, the author instead **incremented it** — "five" became "six" when a ninth case was added — and it remained wrong by exactly the same two, because the count had already missed that one of the cases is a refusal rather than a perturbation and that the script passes two clean extracts rather than one. Incrementing a literal preserves whatever error the literal already carried; only recomputing removes it, and the reason to recompute is precisely that nobody rereads the sentence they are adjusting. The stale number had been correct once, at the commit where it was written, which is the condition that makes this class survive review: every reader who checks it against the moment it was authored finds it sound.

34. A correction and the text it corrects live under opposite rules, and a fix written in the wrong one of the two is invisible to the gate. Rule 22 requires a false claim to stay visible with its refutation adjacent, so the document keeps the original sentence inside a blockquote. Rule 28 requires every quantified claim to be re-derived from the shipped data, and a checker can only anchor on text that asserts something — which the quoted false sentence, by design, does not. The two collide at the exact point they are both doing their job: the corrected figures were first written *inside* the rule-22 quote, next to the wrong ones, where they read perfectly to a human and where the anchors deliberately cannot see them. A correction placed there is unchecked, and unchecked is the state the original defect shipped in. So the discipline is positional: false text stays in the quote, the true replacement goes in live prose outside it, and the anchor is written against the live sentence. This generalises past blockquotes to anywhere a document quotes itself — evidence sections that reproduce a claim verbatim to discuss it are the other common case, and they cut the opposite way, since a whole-file replace aimed at the live claim will hit the quoted copy instead. Both directions were observed in one step: a perturbation case broke because the section documenting it quoted the string it perturbs, and a correction was nearly shipped ungated because it was written beside the sentence it replaced. When a document discusses its own claims, the position of a sentence is part of its meaning, and no checker can recover that from the text alone.

35. Two parties fixing the same defect in parallel will produce different fixes, and the better artifact is not reliably the later one, the longer one, or one's own. The coordinator, told by the implementing session that it had made no changes, wrote and pushed a correction to §5.1; the session had already written its own, unpushed. Both corrected the same false sentence, both derived the replacement from the CSV rather than transcribing it, and both replaced the control's hardcoded count with a computed one. **Neither dominated.** The session's gated the divisibility mechanism, which the coordinator's corrected in prose and left ungated — the weaker half of a commit whose entire argument is that an ungated correction is how the original defect shipped. Its `heap-arm-spread` derived four figures against two, so the four-row subpopulation that the false sentence had actually described became a checked number rather than a claim about a claim. And its helper deduplicated by scenario with the reason in its docstring, the achieved CSV carrying one row per (scenario, factor), so that counting rows would report fifteen distinct values and read as a document defect — rule 32 applied to the checker rather than only to the prose. The coordinator's carried one thing the session's could not, having been written first: binding counted as *equalling the shared minimum* rather than strictly exceeding the other arm, because `SharedMinimumMb` is a `Math.Max` and on a tie both arms bind, so a strict `>` reports a **true** document as false the first time the arms agree. There are no ties in this matrix, so both definitions return 30 and the divergence is invisible — until a third collector arrives and makes ties ordinary. The resolution was to take the better half of each and say in the commit message which half came from where, rather than to pick a winner and lose the rest. Two things follow. Reconcile by reading both diffs against each other before choosing, because "mine, plus whatever theirs has that mine lacks" is a different and better commit than either; and when a competing fix arrives, the parts of it that are stronger than yours are the parts you will be least inclined to look for. The cause was the coordinator's own: a report that nothing had changed was read as a fact about the present rather than a description of a moment, which is the same error as acting on a hash last read some time ago — a rule this coordinator wrote and had twice enforced against the session.

36. A perturbation battery tests only the perturbations someone thought of, so "I watched this check fail" is a weaker guarantee than it sounds. `heap-arm-spread` expected the workstation value set as the literal substring `4, 11, 19, 35, 99`. It was written, anchored, perturbed and watched failing before it was trusted — the perturbation altered a value, `99` to `98`, and the gate duly exited 1 naming only that claim. What nobody tried was **adding** one. A document reading `4, 11, 19, 35, 99, 250 MiB` contains the expected substring, so **a superset passes a check for the set**, and the gate returned exit 0 with `PASS (12 prose claims)` over a document asserting a minimum that does not exist in the matrix. Confirmed by running the same falsified document against both commits rather than by argument: passing at one, failing at the next. Two properties of this make it general. The check was authored in the very commit whose thesis is that an ungated correction is how the original defect ships, by the party that had just documented the expected-3-matching-3.3x class twice — and the same commit reintroduced a bare count, `5`, satisfied by the `4` heading the list it counts, which is that class a third time. Familiarity with a defect class does not confer immunity to it. And the failing perturbation was *representative-looking*: substitution feels like the natural way to falsify a list, so the battery reached a comfortable stopping point while an entire direction of falsification went untested. The defence is to enumerate the *shapes* a claim can be wrong in before choosing perturbations — for a set, at minimum: a changed member, a removed member, an added member, a reordering; for a count, a value too high and too low; for a range, each endpoint independently and the pair inverted — and to prefer expectations that cannot be satisfied by a superstring at all, binding the value to the punctuation or the words that introduce it. Note the asymmetry that makes this worth its own entry rather than a note under rule 28: a check too *strict* announces itself immediately by failing a correct document, and a check too *loose* is silent forever. Every defect in this class found so far has been a loose one.

37. A fact stated twice is gated in one place and unchecked in the other, and the gate cannot tell you which. `find_anchor` returns the **first** non-blockquote match, so a second statement of a gated fact is invisible to the checker by construction — no amount of care writing the check would catch it, because the check passes on the first copy and never looks further. Section 7's carry-forward restated ``srv`` binds in 30 of 30 cells and the arms tie in 0 of 30, both facts section 5.1 states and the prose checker verifies, phrased so the anchor does not match them. Confirmed by running it rather than by argument: falsifying section 7's copy alone, leaving section 5.1 correct, yields `RESULT: PASS (34 checks)` at exit 0. Gating both copies is the wrong repair, and this is the part worth remembering — **a fact stated twice can be right in one place and wrong in the other, with nothing in the artifact able to tell a reader which**, so the duplicate is removed rather than checked: the second statement cites the first and carries no count of its own. Half the duplicate had arrived in the commit that removed a *definitional* duplicate, which is the shape of the thing — the repair of one restatement introduced another. The rule needs a limit or it bans all repetition and guts the evidence sections: a section narrating a defect quotes the counts it came from, and an evidence section reproduces tool output verbatim; both quote a fact rather than assert it. The distinguishing question is whether a reader would take the sentence **as the source of the number**. Where they would, it must be the only place that states it. Related to rule 28 but not a case of it: rule 28 is about a claim no check reads, while this is about a claim a check reads *somewhere else*, which is worse because the gate reports green with specific authority.

38. A check whose correctness depends on a condition the shipped data does not contain cannot be validated against that data — the condition has to be built. `SharedMinimumMb` is a `Math.Max`, so on a tie both arms attain the maximum and a check written around strict `srv > wks` reports a *true* document false. The matrix has **0 ties in 30 rows**, so every perturbation of the shipped CSVs agrees with every perturbation of the wrong definition, and no amount of perturbing the real data distinguishes them. I established this by reasoning from the source and was right; the implementer established it by **constructing the tie** — raising one scenario's Workstation minimum to its Server value, holding `sharedMinimumMb` fixed so the formula claims stayed true by construction, and re-running: strict gives `srv = 27 of 30` while attainment gives `srv 30, wks 3, ties 3`, with exactly the two right checks failing and the binding-count check correctly not failing. The reasoning and the construction reached the same answer, and only one of them is evidence. That is the ungated-correction pattern one level up: a correct fix shipped with nothing showing it is correct. The durable defence is to make the two readings visible in every run rather than trusting that they agree — the checker now prints `strict would give srv=N` beside the attainment count, so the day they diverge is the day it is on screen. **This is not hypothetical for P0.6**: the maximum becomes a three-arm one the moment LXR is added, at which point ties stop being rare, and any check written around strict inequality will fail on true text and read as a prose defect. Second half, from the same commit and the same root: an anchor pinned to a *derived* number has a failure direction worse than rule 33's. Anchoring on `All ten converged` or `take five distinct values` means that when the data moves, **correcting** the document makes the anchor stop matching, so the checker reports the claim **deleted** rather than **changed** — the one edit that should reassure you is the one that looks like sabotage. Anchors must be literal-free: bind to the words that introduce a value, never to the value.

39. A count is not a claim until its unit is stated, and two true counts in different units read as a contradiction. §9 described P0.4's harness as "5 new sources, 12 modified ones, and one `.csproj`" while `git diff --name-status` reports **13 modified**. I published that as a stated count disagreeing with the tool. It was not: `12` counts modified *sources* and `13` counts modified *files*, the `.csproj` being the difference — every number in the original sentence is true, and 5 + 12 + 1 = 18 is the correct total. The real defect was that three labels read as disjoint buckets when two overlap, so the sentence licenses a false inference without asserting a false number. The implementer disputed my framing and was right, and the distinction is load-bearing rather than pedantic: **rule 32's defect is a number false of the population it names, which a checker can re-derive; this one has nothing to re-derive**, since every figure recomputes correctly, so prose-vs-data verification is structurally incapable of catching it and a rule built from rule 32's pattern will not extend to it. The defence is different in kind — state the unit beside the count and make overlapping buckets name their overlap ("13 modified, of which one is a `.csproj` and one is the test file") rather than listing exclusions beside the total. Twice in one step I read a units mismatch as a disagreement: this, and a `MinimumForArm` audit where my line-level count said 1 and the canvas's occurrence-level count said 2, which looked for half a minute like a parse defect and was one line containing the identifier twice. Both times the numbers were right and only the units were missing, and both times my first instinct was to report a defect rather than to ask what was being counted.

40. A verification recipe correct for one artifact can be structurally wrong for another, and the wrong answer arrives as a refusal that reads as a failure. My standing method is to verify from a `git archive` extract outside any worktree, so that what is checked is the committed tree rather than my working directory. That is right for the gate and **impossible** for the control: `verify-gate-of-the-gate.sh` performs its own `git archive` of the committed tree, so it needs a checkout to archive *from*, and in an extract it exits 2 with `not a git checkout, or no git that can read it`. Both the implementer and I hit this independently, each initially reading exit 2 as a failing control on a passing gate. The script is behaving correctly — it refuses rather than passing vacuously, which is the design rule 25 asks for — but a refusal and a failure are the same colour to someone applying a recipe by habit. The rule generalises past this instance: **a tool that consumes its own version control cannot be verified by detaching it from version control**, and any check that reads repository state (citations resolved against files, tree hashes, `ls-files --eol`) has the same shape. State the required environment beside each check rather than assuming one recipe covers the suite — the gate takes an extract, the control takes a checkout at the hash being attested. **Second instance, in a different medium, found while validating the rule floor raised for rule 106.** I copied `board-check.ps1` into the session artifacts directory with the floor set one above the board and ran it as a negative control: exit **2**, and no output line matching `floor`. Read as “non-zero, therefore the control fired” it was a clean pass — in fact `$PSScriptRoot` travelled with the copy, `roadmap.md` was never found, and the floor check never executed. Re-run in place it printed `FAIL rule count 106 is below the floor of 107` at exit **1**. The discriminator this rule needs was already being emitted: **2 is a refusal, 1 is a verdict.** So a negative control must assert the specific failing line it expects, never merely a non-zero exit — and the check it validates must distinguish “could not run” from “ran and rejected” in its exit code, which is the property that made this recoverable at all. **Third instance, same shape, one call later.** Probing the canvas host for the board it serves, `@($r.rules).Count` returned **1** against a state payload that has no `rules` field at all — PowerShell wraps `$null` into a one-element array, so a probe that cannot see its subject reports a plausible count instead of nothing. It survived only because 1 is absurd for a 106-rule board; had the expected answer been 1, it would have passed silently and I would have reported the served board as verified. What the three instances share is the generalization worth carrying: **a probe must distinguish “the subject is absent” from “the subject measured zero”**, and neither a non-zero exit code nor an array count does that by default — so the assertion has to name something only a real measurement could produce.

41. `git status` reports agreement with a ref, not agreement with the work, and a branch reset onto a remote is indistinguishable from one that always matched it. Through the late corrections of P0.5 the implementer and I were rewriting the same commit range simultaneously — it amending its tip, me re-implementing its content on top of what I had already pushed. That resolved cleanly and it should not be mistaken for a safe process: it worked **only because the two trees converged**. Had they differed anywhere except the one sentence we happened to fix independently, `reset --hard` onto the pushed ref would have silently discarded whatever the other party had and nothing would have shown it — the losing branch reports clean, the winning branch reports pushed, and the diff that would reveal the loss is one nobody runs because nothing looks wrong. The concrete defence is cheap: **diff the trees before resetting**, and if you intend to re-implement a collaborator's work rather than take their commits, say so, because their default is to keep amending the tip you last read. The same episode supplies the positive form. Two independently-authored sequences — four commits and eight, neither an ancestor of the other — produced byte-identical trees at `9f68f071f29ca01a2cf137a27a62aad39256a10c`. **Convergent tree hashes from disjoint histories are a stronger attestation than either party verifying alone**, because agreement cannot have come from copying a verdict; it is the one form of confirmation in this project that does not depend on trusting a report. Prefer `rev-parse '<rev>^{tree}'` over commit hashes whenever the question is whether two things are the same work, which is also the only way to verify across a squash merge.

42. A checker that derives every expectation from data cannot check a claim about the document's own structure, and such claims should be marked ungated rather than left silently unchecked. §5.1 introduced its list as `Two consequences` while three items followed: the list gained the tie consequence at my request and the lead-in was never touched, so the very section that documents *a stated figure disagreeing with the thing beside it* shipped carrying an instance of it. Gating this is not a small addition — every prose claim re-derives its expected value from a shipped CSV, and counting a list's items is a **second mechanism** inside a checker built around one. The right resolution is to fix the count and record that it is deliberately ungated, because an unchecked claim that is known and labelled is a different object from one nobody has thought about. The general bound: **a gate proves the claims it was built to derive, and its passing says nothing about any other kind of claim in the same document** — lead-ins, list counts, cross-references, type names, and section numbering are all outside it, so a document is never "verified" merely because its gate is green. The companion defect in the same commit was `HeapBaselines.SharedMinimumMb`, a **type** name that names no member: `SharedMinimumMb` is an instance member of `HeapBaseline` while the static `HeapBaselines` holds `LimitMb` and `For(...)`. Identifiers in prose are claims about the tree and nothing re-derives them either.

43. The verification tooling has its own defaults, and a count produced with the wrong one is indistinguishable from a defect in the thing being counted. PowerShell's `-match`, `-like`, `-replace`, `-eq` and `Select-String` are **case-insensitive by default**; only the `-c`-prefixed forms (`-cmatch`, `-creplace`) and `Select-String -CaseSensitive` are not. Counting `Claim\(` in the prose checker returned **13** against a script that derives **12**, and for about a minute that looked like a real discrepancy in a number this project has re-verified repeatedly. It was `derive_floor_claim(` — a function name whose tail matches the constructor when case is ignored. `-cmatch` returns 12 and everything agrees. This matters beyond the one instance because identifiers are the thing most often grepped when verifying a claim about source, and case is exactly what distinguishes a type from a member from a local in every language in this repo, so the default silently merges categories that the code deliberately separates. **Use `-cmatch` for any count of an identifier**, and treat a count that disagrees with a derived value as a suspected defect *in the count* until the matching semantics have been checked — rule 39's discipline applied one level down, to the instrument rather than the measurement. Nearly reporting this as a defect in the implementer's work would have been the same error I had spent the step correcting in it. **The implementer supplied the mirror instance, and I had already committed it without noticing.** Counting the tie value by grepping `0 of 30` returns **15**, because `0 of 30` is a substring of `30 of 30` and thirteen of the hits state the binding-arm count instead; the anchored count is **2**. I ran exactly that grep, printed all fifteen lines under a heading claiming they stated "the tie count in any form", and read past it because I had already isolated the two occurrences I was looking for in the block above. So the defect was not that the grep misled me — it did not — but that I published its output under a description only two lines satisfied. **An unanchored pattern answers a different question from the one asked, and answers it loudly**, which is the same class as the case-insensitive count: the instrument silently widens the category, and a wide answer is more convincing than a narrow one because it has more evidence in it.

44. A subtree hash carries an expensive attestation forward across every commit that does not touch it, which is the cheapest verification instrument this project has. The harness suite is slow to build and run, and P0.5's result was established at one hash with five further commits landing above it. Rather than re-running, `git rev-parse <hash>:docs/design/lxr-port/harness` at each: **`dfc395e68d34` at all six**, so the result attaches to the head without a second run. This is tree-identity from rule 41 applied to a subtree and to a *result* rather than to a comparison, and it answers the question that actually matters after a late fix — not "did the tree change" but "did anything I have evidence about change". It also states the negative precisely: the same command proves those commits touched only `.md` and two scripts, so no reasoning is required about whether a documentation fix could have perturbed a test. Record the subtree hash beside every expensive result, because an attestation without one is pinned to a commit and dies at the next amend. The count itself belongs in the step's evidence field and is not restated here, per rule 37.

45. The harness can only be built by an SDK that is not on the PATH, and it writes its output outside itself when moved. Rule 31 already records that `dotnet test` reports success here without executing anything; these are the two environment facts that sit beside it, each of which cost a turn to rediscover. The projects target `net11.0`, so the machine-wide 10.0 SDK fails them with `NETSDK1045`, and the only SDK that can build them is the one `global.json` pins — which exists on this machine solely inside a session worktree's `.dotnet` directory, not on the PATH and not in Program Files. More consequentially, `Directory.Build.props` derives `ArtifactsPath` from `HarnessRepoRoot`, computed by walking **four levels up** from the harness directory. That is correct in its repository position and silently wrong everywhere else: an extract placed elsewhere writes build output into whatever directory happens to sit four levels above it, and mine landed in the user's home directory. So the extract-based recipe of rule 40 is not merely inapplicable to the harness but **actively unsafe**, and the three defects together — this, rule 31's silent pass, and P0.4's worktree-hostile control script — mean the harness cannot currently be verified by any method this project actually uses. All three are P0.6 work.

46. A battery needs an assertion at **both** ends, because observing only one verdict cannot distinguish a working check from a broken battery. Observing only FAIL cannot tell "the check fired" from "the harness never reached the document"; observing only PASS cannot tell "no defect" from "the perturbation did not apply". The implementer hit the first end for real: invoking the prose checker with `--results` pointing one directory too deep produced **exit 1 with five `FAIL missing input` lines on a completely unperturbed tree**. A battery that scored FAIL as success would have reported four checks firing while the checker had never read the document. I reproduced it and proposed a discriminator — the broken run emits `exit≠0` with ZERO anchored `^RESULT:` lines, a genuinely fired check emits `exit≠0` with exactly ONE `^RESULT: FAIL` — **and the implementer defeated it, correctly.** Point `--doc` at a different but *valid* document with `--results` still correct: every anchor misses, so the checker emits a real verdict line, and my discriminator scores `RESULT: FAIL (12 of 12 prose claims disagree with the data)` as a healthy battery with all twelve checks firing, while it never read the document under test. `--doc` and `--results` are the two arguments of one invocation and they fail in opposite directions. Reproduced at `9f054925372`, five rows from one run: pristine `PASS (12)` exit 0; `--results` one level too deep, exit 1, 0 anchored, 5 `FAIL missing input`; `--doc` nonexistent, exit 1, 0 anchored; `--doc` valid-but-wrong, exit 1, **1 anchored, `12 of 12`**; genuine one-claim perturbation, exit 1, 1 anchored, `1 of 12`. **The guard that covers all five is a quantity, not a presence: assert that the fired count equals the perturbed count.** Zero anchored lines fails "equals one" as surely as `12 of 12` does, so the count subsumes the presence test rather than supplementing it. **The count-equality guard has its own precondition, found by running it on the `:468` probe: it presupposes you perturbed a string you expect to be gated.** Perturbing `:468` yields perturbed 1, fired 0 — which the guard reads as a broken battery and which is in fact the finding, that the occurrence is ungated. When the question is *whether* a string is gated, zero fired is the answer; when the question is whether the battery works, zero fired is the malfunction. Same numbers, and only the intent distinguishes them, so state which question you are asking before reading the count. **Bounded by an exhaustive trace, the shipped gate is immune to both:** `verify-baselines.sh` invokes the checker exactly once, at `:288`, as `--doc "$DOC" --results "$BASE"`, and both derive from `$ROOT` (`:77`, `:78`); the user-supplied `--results` binds to `RESULTS_DIR`, whose every use is locating checkpoint JSON at `:149` and printing the mode. The hazard therefore lives in ad-hoc batteries, which is where both of us met it, and the P0.5 deliverable is unaffected. Two repairs a later reader might wrongly draw from this rule: do **not** stop the gate branching on the checker's exit code at `:288`, because the exit code is the checker's designed interface for a *consumer* and the count matters only for a *battery* deciding whether a check fired; and do **not** thread `--results` through to the prose checker, because prose must be re-derived from the CSVs shipped beside the document rather than from a directory named on the command line.

47. When a check rejects true prose, whether that is a defect turns on **what can reach the false positive**, and the two cases need opposite responses. The arm-spread list check is order-sensitive: a document naming the same five minima in a different order is rejected, which I confirmed at the head — `4, 11, 35, 19, 99` fails while `4, 11, 19, 35, 99` passes, same set, same count. That looks identical in shape to the strict-`>` tie defect, where the checker would also have rejected a true document, and yet the right answers differ.
