The distinguishing test is whether the false positive **arrives on its own as data moves**: the tie fires when nobody has touched the prose, so it is a defect and had to be fixed; a reordering can only appear if an author deliberately writes a non-canonical rendering, so it is a **canonical-form constraint** and should be documented rather than relaxed. Loosening it would cost the property that makes the check worth having, since an order-insensitive set comparison is a short step from the substring match that let a superset through. Record the constraint where the next author will meet it, because the failure reads as a false alarm to anyone who has not been told it is deliberate.
48. **A duplicate cleared by "the checker does not see it" has been cleared by its own defect.** The P0.5 session audited section 5.1 for the duplication defect we had just removed from section 7, found a second statement of the gated tie count, and cleared it on the grounds that the gate's anchor matches the source line first and the second sentence is a different string. That invisibility is the rule-37 condition itself, not a clearance: a restatement the gate cannot see is precisely the one that goes stale silently while the gated copy fails loudly and gets corrected. The test stays rule 37's — would a reader take this sentence as the source of the number — and it is answered by reading, not by asking what the checker matches. I verified the reasoning rather than the verdict, which is the only reason it surfaced; a negative report is as reviewable as a positive one and deserves the same treatment.
49. **Rank duplicates by whether the fact is predicted to move, and the worst one will be inside the paragraph predicting it.** The restatement removed here sat in the consequence titled "Ties stop being hypothetical" — a paragraph written to warn that P0.6's third arm makes ties real — and the value it restated was the tie count. So the sentence would have gone stale in exactly the scenario it exists to anticipate, and the more the warning is heeded the sooner its own number becomes false. A duplicate of a stable fact is untidy; a duplicate of a fact the document itself forecasts changing is a scheduled defect with a known trigger date. When time is short, grep the restated values against the things the document says will change. **Bounded by the implementer, correctly, on the paragraph that generated it: rank by whether the fact is predicted to move, except where the sentence's assertion *is* the prediction.** Applied naively the rule selects `:468` first — an ungated second occurrence of a gated count, sitting inside the very paragraph forecasting that count will change, which is every condition the rule names at once. It is immune, because staleness is what it asserts: "a checker written around strict inequality reports the *correct* sentence "`srv` is the binding arm in 30 of 30" as false the first time two arms tie". A tie does not falsify that, it demonstrates it. And the repair destroys the sentence, since the quoted count is the grammatical object of "reports as false" — remove it and a checker reports *the correct sentence*, naming nothing. Contrast the restatement actually removed, "the tie count is published **at 0 of 30**", which asserted a present value: same paragraph, same number, opposite exposure. Audited the whole class rather than the one line, because the rule is only worth having if it partitions: `binding arm in 30 of 30` occurs **6** times, and perturbing each shows `:423` fires `FAIL (1 of 12)` while `:468` leaves `PASS (12)`. Of the five ungated, `:468` and `:1064` are prediction sentences and `:984`, `:1003` and `:1094` are §9 narration naming the string as a string — mentioned, not used. **No live defect among them, and the two exempt classes are prediction and citation.** State the bound explicitly, because the sentence most likely to trip the rule is the one that exists to state it.
50. **Resolve a ref at the moment of use rather than from memory — but check the clock before charging anyone with staleness.** I first recorded this rule against the P0.5 session for "re-verifying against `e68c3daa489`, the direct parent of its own fix". The method advice is right; **the attribution was wrong and I withdraw it.** Inter-session delivery was lagging by tens of minutes, and at the moment that check was composed `e68c3daa489` *was* origin — the verification was correct when written and stale only on arrival, which is a property of the channel and not of its method. What survives is the practice that makes a report robust to a slow channel: resolve with `git ls-remote` at the point of use, state the hash you checked against as well as the finding, and prefer a subtree or tree hash, which stays true regardless of when the message lands. **A second instance shows the advice is necessary but not sufficient: the durable hash has to be bound to an immutable ref, or one moving conjunct spoils the whole assurance.** Asked a third time to state the search behind its `Aggregator.cs` = 15 count, the P0.5 session did everything this rule asks and more — it named a **blob**, stronger than the subtree hash recommended here: *“Blob `7cab0c6ecbb` at `9f054925372`, `6cdeea5ba1e` **and HEAD**, so it isn't ref drift on my side either.”* Verified against the object store: the count is **15** on `(?i)pause`, and both line lists are exact at that blob — **10 comment** at `:59 :64 :65 :66 :69 :73 :301 :303 :329 :331` and **5 code** at `:338 :423 :424 :425 :430`, matching character for character. **Every claim was true when written, and one of them is false now.** The blob at today's `0f685359c1c` is `a8b83893305`, so the same search returns `329 331 338 423 424 425 430` shifted to `330 332 339 424 425 426 431`. Two of the three conjuncts are permanent because commit refs are immutable; the third named `HEAD`, and **`blob B at commit C` is a fact while `blob B at HEAD` has a shelf life.** The moving conjunct was also redundant — the two fixed refs already carried the entire argument, so dropping it would have cost nothing and the assurance would still be true today. **What falsified an assurance against ref drift was ref drift, committed by its own author between writing and reading**, and the commit that did it is `17e7aacb42b`, *“three finding ids cited from shipped code resolve to no document”* — a commit about citations that do not resolve, which broke a citation by adding two comment lines while fixing one. This is F26's shape, which that session defended as rot rather than narration-ahead and was right to: **rot is a claim that was true and stopped being true, and the fix for rot is never re-reading before shipping — it is an anchor that does not move.** **Three further instances arrived within the hour, one mine and two the P0.5 session's, and between them they show that closing sentence is half right and names the wrong remedy for the other half.** Mine first, because it is the worse one: one commit after boarding the paragraph above, I wrote into P0.5's entry *“PR #5 is at `9f054925372` and the branch **is** at `0f685359c1c`, seventeen commits above it”*. The hash is pinned, the count is correct against it, and the sentence was false within the hour — the branch was `7c725de8fc8` at nineteen. **The anchor was right and did nothing, because the noun in front of it was “the branch”.** An anchor fixes the *object* of a claim and has no reach over a moving *subject*; I had pinned the thing being pointed at and left the pointer free. Fixed in `b4418bb9bf2` by naming both observations with their hashes, calling the count a floor, and publishing `git rev-list --count 9f054925372..HEAD` so the live figure is computed rather than remembered. **The other two are the P0.5 session's, verified read-only at `7c725de8fc8` rather than accepted.** F26's own hand-correction rotted a second time: the anchored `grep -c '^RESULT: PASS'` it cites sits at `:177`, while the hand-fixed `:154` holds `case "$want_exit" in` and the original `:132` holds a comment — **both non-blank, so the gate passed over both**, which is F26's own finding surviving its own repair. A correction found by accident and not swept resets the clock; it does not remedy the class. **The fifth instance is the one this rule could not have predicted: F39's `check-prose-claims.py:143` was true against `7c725de8fc8^` and false in `7c725de8fc8` itself.** The cited line — `affected.add((r["scenario"], r["collector"], r["mode"], …))` — is at `:143` in the parent and `:245` in the commit, and that commit's first hunk is `@@ -114,0 +115,102 @@`: **+102 above old line 143, and 143+102=245 exactly.** Here *re-reading before shipping* is not a weak remedy, it is an **unavailable** one — there is no instant between writing and committing at which a re-read returns the right line, because the citation and its target moved in the same diff. So rot has three mechanisms and the prescribed remedy covers one and a half of them: **target moves after shipping** (anchor works), **target moves in the same commit as the citation** (anchor works, re-reading provably cannot), **subject moves while the object stays pinned** (anchor is correct and irrelevant). **My own sweep of the third needs its own correction, and it points the same way as everything else here.** I ran the citation audit with the resolver rooted at `docs/design/lxr-port/P0.5-baselines` while the harness sits a level up at `docs/design/lxr-port/harness`, and got 13 distinct citations with **9 unresolvable** — a 69% failure rate that I would have read as a finding about the document. Re-rooted at the port tree: **17 occurrences, 15 distinct, 0 unresolvable, 0 failing the gate's predicate**, and both rotted citations inside that population. I still do not reach the session's 27, so the populations disagree about the pattern — but the finding is robust to that, and *sharper* on the narrower net: 2 of 15 rather than 2 of 27. **A resolver rooted below its targets reports the document as broken; the same defect that makes a citation unresolvable makes the auditor confident.** Note last that neither session prompted the other — we were fixing instances of one defect, in different artifacts, in the same hour, each having just boarded it. So the practice extends by one clause: name the durable hash, and pin it to a ref that cannot change, never to `HEAD`, `main`, or `origin/*`.
51. **Under delivery lag, the absence of a report is not evidence that none was sent — and a coordinator with filesystem access to a child will always see its work before its words.** I found `3cadda3d54f` by running `git worktree list` during cleanup, read it as an unpushed commit the session had not mentioned, and told it twice that it had lost track of its own work and that its `git status` hazard had turned inward. Its announcement arrived **47 minutes later**, carrying the hash, a three-line diff, gate and control results, and an offer to `git reset --hard` the commit away: it had reported within a minute of authoring. I also recorded that my replies were generating the repetition and instructed it to stop replying — but re-stating findings that cannot be confirmed received is the correct behaviour on a lossy channel, and the session said so in plain terms ("three status reports failed to get them to you"). **Default to "the message is in flight", never to "it concealed the work"**, and keep acknowledgements short and early, because a long one composed while the next report is already being written cannot arrive in time to stop it. This is the third time I have rewritten this theory; each rewrite discarded a true cause on encountering another, which is rule 49's error in a different costume. The queue also drains out of order and keeps draining after a stand-down: I have now received **three** separate messages announcing 3cadda3d54f as unpushed, every one composed before I pushed it and none mentioning the head that superseded it. So verify state and stop — do not answer each arrival as a fresh round, because every answer adds a turn to a queue that is already behind, and the state check costs one command while the reply costs a round trip on both sides. *This rule replaced a different claim under the same number and did not say so.* Its first version read — **“When a child re-sends materially the same message after a correcting reply, the reply is what is producing it”** — a diagnosis of a reply loop that did not exist, withdrawn at `be5bc610e00` in the same commit as rule 50’s staleness charge. Rule 22 requires the original be quoted when a claim is corrected in place; rules 50 and 98 do, this one did not for eleven days, and the omission was found by the history check that rule 103 motivated — the guard caught a real defect on its first run rather than a hypothetical one.
52. **A hash in prose is untyped, and reading a tree as a commit produces a confident false correction.** I published `495a4d5f1b3` as the tree of the commit being pushed. The P0.5 session read it as a commit, found nothing above `3cadda3d54f` on origin, and drafted a note telling me my branch pointer was wrong — then ran `git cat-file -t`, got `tree`, and confirmed `rev-parse 3cadda3d54f^{tree}` matched it exactly. Every git object name lives in one 40-hex namespace, so nothing in the string distinguishes a commit from a tree or a blob, and the failure mode is quiet rather than loud: `rev-parse` resolves it happily, while `log` and `merge-base` reject it in terms that read as "not on this branch" — which is indistinguishable from the branch pointer being wrong. **Run `git cat-file -t` before treating a hash you did not produce as a commit, and name the type when publishing one.** This is rule 39's shape arriving from the other side within minutes of that rule being written: the disagreement was real, and it was a unit error rather than a defect.
53. **A battery's self-check is a checker, and inherits every failure mode of the checks it supervises.** Rule 46 asked *is there a verdict line* where the discriminating fact is *how many fired* — presence substituted for occurrence, which is rule 36's superset satisfying a check for a set and rule 36's bare `5` satisfied by the `4` heading the list it counts, now recurring inside the tool built to catch them. Nothing exempts the supervisory layer: run on it the checks you run on what it supervises. I then supplied the instance from the other end, while testing that very case — `$args` is a PowerShell **automatic variable**, so `function Run($label, $args)` bound nothing, `@args` splatted empty, and all four cases silently ran the same unperturbed invocation and returned an identical `PASS (12 prose claims)`, including two that must fail. Reading only the uniform PASS would have confirmed the defeated rule and shipped it. Count-equality catches this too — perturbed 1, fired 0 — which is a second and independent argument for preferring it: it constrains the result rather than enumerating the ways a harness can break, so it is the one assertion that survives a battery broken in a way nobody anticipated.
54. **A backtick is markdown's code delimiter and PowerShell's escape character, so writing board text through a double-quoted string silently destroys every code span in it.** Appending to P0.6's entry that way produced, from one line, `` `re.IGNORECASE` `` → `<CR>e.IGNORECASE`, `` `find_anchor` `` → `<FF>ind_anchor` and `` `theta` `` → `<TAB>heta`: measured on a 53-character sample, the double-quoted form came back **47 characters with zero backticks and one CR, one FF and one TAB injected**, each control character having eaten the identifier's first letter. Three things make it worse than an ordinary typo. The injected bare CR is a line terminator to `ReadAllLines`, so the line silently splits and `git diff` reports the file as a whole-scale rewrite — 682 insertions against 682 deletions — which sent me looking at line endings, the wrong layer entirely, and `i/lf w/crlf text=auto` all checked out fine. A trailing backtick escapes the closing quote, so the failure sometimes arrives as an unrelated parse error dozens of lines later; that happened twice while trying to demonstrate the effect, which is the demonstration. And nothing about the result looks wrong in a commit message or a summary, so it ships. **Use the `edit` tool for prose, or single quotes and `@' '@` literal here-strings when scripting it**; the four board commits made through the edit tool changed 2, 3, 2 and 6 lines, which is what a correct edit looks like. Caught only because the format contract's trailing-whitespace check ran afterwards and flagged a line ending in a space — a check written for a cosmetic rule catching a content-corruption bug, which is the argument for running the cheap structural checks even when the edit "obviously" cannot have broken them.
55. **A rule written here reaches nobody who needs it: a spawned session reads only its kickoff prompt, so a kickoff must name, by number, the rules its step will exercise.** Every kickoff this project has issued — P0.1 through P0.5 — cited zero rule numbers, because `## Operating rules` sits fifty-odd entries deep in a file a child has no reason to open, and none of them opened it. The cost is measurable in P0.5 alone: the child independently rediscovered the presence-for-occurrence substitution and the unanchored-grep hazard *after* both were written down here as rules 53 and 43, spending a round each on findings it could have been handed for free. Name the numbers rather than paraphrasing them, because a paraphrase is a second copy that goes stale on its own schedule — rule 46 was rewritten twice inside one day, first around count-equality and then bounded with a precondition and with the shipped gate's immunity, so a kickoff that had paraphrased its original form would have handed the child the exact version that same child had already defeated. The general defect is broader than kickoffs: an invariant parked in one step's entry binds that step and nothing after it, which is how both the anchor-uniqueness check and the rules-46/49/53/54 requirement began life as P0.6 habits rather than rules, and promoting them here is what makes them bind every later step instead of only the next one. This rule is that promotion applied to itself.
56. **The `edit` tool reports "File updated with changes" for a no-op, so an edit is confirmed by the diff, not by the tool's success message.** Removing a blank line before rule 55, I passed an `old_str` and a `new_str` that were character-identical — both began with a single newline where the fix required the search string to begin with two — and the tool reported success. The file was unchanged: `git diff` produced the identical hunk and, decisively, the same blob hash `08d8e39d1b9` before and after, which is the only signal that distinguished "the edit applied" from "the edit matched nothing that needed changing". This is rules 46 and 53 once more, in the tool used to write the rules themselves: a success report confirms the call was well-formed, not that the intended change occurred, exactly as an exit code confirms a checker ran rather than that it read the right document. The remedy is the same shape as count-equality — assert the *result*, not the report: read the diff after every edit, and prefer an `old_str` that spans the boundary being changed (here, the tail of rule 54 plus the blank plus the head of rule 55) over one anchored on a single side, because a one-sided anchor is what let an identical pair look like a valid edit. The same reading turned up a second instance beside it: the rule-numbering scan matches `^\d+\. ` line by line and so passed 55 rules with no gaps in both layouts, being structurally blind to the blank-line change it sat next to — a check answering a different question loudly, which is rule 43.
57. **Compression preserves figures while deleting the clauses that scope them, so every number carried through a rewrite must be re-checked against its new neighbours.** The P0.5 PR body was cut from 5,170 words to 432 on the user's instruction, and `5 files added, 13 modified` survived into a sentence introducing the *deliverable*, where it is wrong. Both numbers were right as computed: the PR adds 43 files and modifies 14, of which `P0.5-baselines/` is **38 added and 0 modified**, the harness is **5 added and 13 modified**, and `P0.4-harness.md` is the fourteenth. The figure had been measured for the harness and the compression removed the clause saying so, re-binding a correct count to the wrong subject. That is harder to catch than a wrong number, because nothing local contradicts it — the arithmetic is sound and the source is real, and only recomputing the named subject exposes it. It is rule 39 from the other side: there, a count that disagreed might still have been a unit nobody asked about; here, a count that agrees perfectly is reported about something else. The second half is the handoff. The rewrite arrived with an explicit list of eight figures to re-verify and five deleted strings to confirm absent, and all thirteen checked out exactly — because **a battery drawn up by the author of a change inherits that author's blind spot**, and the single defect sat in the one figure the list did not name. Verify what a summary *asserts*, not only what its author thought to flag; the items volunteered for checking are selected by the same understanding that produced the error. The implementer sharpened this afterwards and the sharpened form is the operational one: the list was not a battery that happened to miss a case, it enumerated the figures the rewrite **preserved**, so by construction it could not cover the one figure the rewrite **changed** — and changed is where the defect lives. **When reporting an edit, list what you changed and let the reader check what survived.** That turns a caution about blind spots into a testable instruction, and it explains why a wholly accurate list still gave false assurance: every item on it was true, and the set was chosen by the wrong criterion. My own confirmation carried the same shape one level down — I counted the deliverable with the pattern `docs/design/lxr-port/P0\.5-baselines`, which is unanchored at its end and so matches both the directory and `P0.5-baselines.md`; the total of 38 was right only because the sentence's subject happens to be the union of the two, and it took the implementer's `37 + 1` partition to show the looseness and the subject coincided rather than the count being right by construction.
58. **Verify the consequence, not only the mechanism: the mechanism decides whether a defect exists, the consequence decides what you do about it, and a report can be exactly right about the first and wrong about the second.** The implementer traced a real defect in `verify-baselines.sh` — `--results` selects which checkpoints are audited (`:149`) while every data check reads `$BASE` (`:249`, `:270`, `:288`), so the two halves of one comparison come from two roots — and I confirmed all of it by reading. Attached to it was the assessment that the unsafe case is a rerun whose checkpoint filenames match the committed ones, which "can pass while never reading what you pointed it at". That part is false, and it is the part that drives the decision: `rederive-statistics.py` places three unconditional `return 1`s before its single `PASS`, failing on `checked_mean == 0` when the join produces nothing (`:226`), on `unmatched_cells` for a partial join (`:229`) and on `mismatches` for a full one (`:232`), so every manifestation of a split root fails loudly and a silent pass needs a fresh run to reproduce the committed numbers within a 1e-4 tolerance across every mean field. The flag is **unusable, not dangerous** — which turns "interrupt the merge and fix it now" into "fix it as P0.6's first tooling change", the opposite action. Note also that the implementer's own demonstration, a decoy directory yielding `FAIL (28 passed, 2 failed)`, is evidence for the *safe* direction and was offered as evidence for the dangerous one; a demonstration confirms the mechanism it exercises, not the severity claimed around it. And `:226` is count-equality (rule 46) already shipped by the script's own author, arrived at independently, which is the strongest support that pattern has. **The `28 passed, 2 failed` figure is no longer taken on report — it is reproduced here:** a minimal `{}` decoy under `--results` yields exactly that, the two failures being `schemaVersion is None` and `no decoy-invocations.csv`, which confirms both the number and that the mechanism fails closed.
59. **A gate that only compares can only catch mismatches; nothing in it catches a smaller input set.** `verify-baselines.sh` builds its checkpoint list with `find "$RESULTS_DIR"` (`:149`) and contributes one `ok` per checkpoint inside the loop at `:244-259`, so a supplied directory holding a correctly-named **subset** yields `RESULT: PASS (30 checks)` at exit 0 where the full set yields 34 — every check honest, every number re-derived, two thirds of the evidence never examined, and the banner still reading `mode: full audit`. This defeats my own universal: I declined to treat the `--results` split as dangerous because a split root "fails loudly in every case I could construct", and all four of those cases turn on a **mismatch** — differing names, empty join, partial join, differing numbers — while this one contains no mismatch at all. The defect is absence of coverage rather than presence of a fault, and no comparison fires on an absence. That is rule 57 one level up, and it lands on the author of rule 58: I verified the consequence, then bounded it by an enumeration selected by the same model of the tool that produced the claim. The bound on the fix is the script's own design principle at `:10-11` — *"Expected counts are DERIVED from the artifact, never repeated as literals at several assertion sites, so two cannot drift from a third unnoticed"* — which is precisely why no literal `3` guards the input set: **the principle that prevents brittle assertions and the hole are the same fact**, the second time on this gate that an immunity and a defect have turned out to be one property. Note also what the author did reach: `:414` names-vs-present, `:449` citations-vs-resolved, `:502` committed-vs-recomputed, each comparing two derived quantities and printing the difference. Five arrivals at count-equality in one repository, and the input set still unasserted — because every one of them compares two descriptions of **the same set** (contents) and none asserts that it is **the right set** (extent). The fix that respects `:10` derives the expected count from the artifact too, comparing checkpoints found against checkpoints the document names, in the exact shape of `:414`. **Assert the extent of the input set, derived, or the verdict's scope is unasserted no matter how many of its contents agree.** Discharged against my own board battery the moment the rule was written, because it had the identical gap: it asserted phases, steps, rule numbering, whitespace and control characters — all *contents* — and never the size of the field set, so an edit that clobbered a `- **Status:**` line in a step I wasn't looking at would have passed every check. Measured: **360 fields parse, 358 of them inside the 54 steps, 0 steps missing `Status`, 0 missing `Summary`, 6 ≤ fields per step ≤ 10.** The literal `360` is the part that goes stale the moment P0.6 adds a step, so the standing invariants are the derived ones — *every step carries a non-empty `Status` and `Summary`*, and *the step-field sum plus the phase-level fields equals the total* — which hold at any size. **Reproduced here rather than taken on report:** one real checkpoint under `--results` gives `PASS (30 checks)` exit 0 with the banner still reading `full audit`, against `PASS (34 checks)` for the same tree with no flag. Three decoy variants all produced **30 total checks** and differed only in the pass/fail split, so the total is a function of the input set's *size* and not its *content* — which is what makes count-equality the right guard here rather than merely a plausible one.
60. **When a discrepancy equals a structural count of the document, suspect the method before the artifact.** The implementer's `442` words against my `429` for one PR body differed by exactly `13`, which is the body's blank-line count. PowerShell hands multi-line command output back as an `Object[]` of lines — `gh pr view --json body --jq '.body'` returns **34 elements, not one string** — and `-split` applied to an array runs **per element**, so every blank line contributes one empty string to the total. Reproduced against the live body: naive split `442`, empties dropped `429`, `-join` then split `429`, `[regex]::Matches('\S+')` `429`, blank lines `13`, delta `13`. Note what identified the cause: not three methods outvoting one, but **the delta equalling a count the document already publishes**, which names the defect rather than merely outnumbering it. The underlying mechanism is this shell's array/scalar duality, and we hit it within the same hour **from opposite sides** — I wrote `$r57[0].Length` expecting a line and got `1`, because a single `Where-Object` match comes back as a bare string and `[0]` indexed a character. Assumed-array-got-scalar and assumed-scalar-got-array, one duality, one session. The guard is to force the shape before measuring: `@()` around anything counted, `-join` before any whole-text operation, `[regex]` over a string made scalar on purpose — and never read a shell's convenience reshaping as the shape of the data.
61. **Settle what a flag means before writing a guard for it, and enumerate the flag surface first — the coherent mechanism may already exist and the flag may be deletable rather than fixable.** `verify-baselines.sh` accepts exactly two long options — `--results` (`:42`) and `--no-results` (`:51`) — rejects every other `--*` at `:59`, and takes one positional `ROOT_ARG` (`:64`); `:77-79` then derive `DOC`, `BASE` and `HARNESS` from that single `$ROOT` **together**. So auditing a different tree *coherently* is already supported and always was: pass the positional. `--results` is **not** the only construct in the script that can split the roots — I wrote that and it is false. `$SELF_DIR` (`:34`) is a second root, and the two checks at `:193` and `:407` assert facts about the **audited** tree while reading the **apparatus** tree: `:193` tests `$SELF_DIR/run-p05-baselines.ps1` and concludes *"the run script ships with the results it produced"*, and `:407` tests `$SELF_DIR/$script` over names `:401` derived from `$ROOT`'s document — so `:414`, the very check I proposed as the model for the fix, is itself split-rooted. Note `:74`: with no positional, `ROOT` is derived *from* `$SELF_DIR`, so the roots coincide and the split is inert — the third construct on this gate whose immunity and defect are one fact. What `--results` is, is the only construct whose split was *undisclosed*; `:145` prints `self:` beside `root:`, so this one is deliberate and announced, and it is right for **executing** the apparatus and wrong only for these two checks that read it as evidence. That reframes the fork the implementer identified. **A** — *audit the committed document against another results tree* — is a real reproducibility check, and making it coherent means moving every data root to `$RESULTS_DIR` while the document stays committed; under it, a document-derived expectation for the checkpoint set is right and a mismatch **must** fail. **B** — *audit another tree on its own terms* — is the positional argument, and needs no flag at all. The defect was never the plumbing: **the flag has never had a stated meaning, and the code implements neither reading.** This lands on me. I recorded a `:414`-shaped guard as the fix without settling which reading it enforced; under A it is correct and under B it fires on every legitimate use, so I had written a check that votes on an unsettled interface without noticing it was voting. Note also what this costs P0.6: its stated first use — gate a fresh session — is B, so it wants the positional rather than `--results`, and even that is blocked because `:77-79` hardcode `P0.5-baselines.md` and `P0.5-baselines/` into the derivation. Correction to the implementer's framing, for the record: this script has **no `--doc` flag**; `--doc` belongs to `check-prose-claims.py`, so B cannot be expressed here by pairing `--doc` with `--results`, only by the positional.
62. **Re-verify a child session when the input that arrived could plausibly change the state, not when something merely arrived.** A bare idle notification carries no content and authorizes nothing, so it is not a reason to re-run `git rev-parse`; a message asking for work is. I stated this bound twice and it was ambiguous against its own instance both times, because I wrote it as *"a new input from me"* while my own closing and declining messages are inputs that cannot authorize a commit. The purposive form terminates and the mechanical one does not: **check when the arriving input could cause the change you are checking for.** Under it, four verifications of the same no-commit instruction were three too many, and the one that mattered was the first — immediately after countermanding the child's offer to fix, which is the only moment the instruction was under live pressure.
63. **A verdict has three things it can get wrong — its contents, its extent, and its subject — and count-equality reaches only the first two.** The implementer demonstrated the third with a paired control: a copy of the tree at HEAD with `check-calibration.py` deleted, audited from *this* checkout via the positional, returns `PASS (34 checks)` exit 0 and prints `ok document names 6 script(s), 6 present, difference 0`; the same perturbed tree audited by *its own* copy of the gate returns `FAIL (32 passed, 2 failed) missing: check-calibration.py`. Same tree, same perturbation, opposite verdicts, decided only by which copy of the apparatus you invoke. Both runs carry 34 `ok` lines, so rule 59's extent assertion cannot see it and neither can rule 46 — the subset case *loses* checks, this one keeps every check and gets one **wrong**, reporting a true statement about the wrong subject. **This is the silent mis-verification I argued could not happen** when I ruled the `--results` split inert; it exists, in the construct I had just called coherent, and it took someone else building the control to produce it. The rule that follows is the split itself: **trusted apparatus, suspect artifact** — execution paths belong on `$SELF_DIR` and every assertion *about* the audited tree belongs on `$BASE`/`$ROOT`, so `:193` and `:407` are simply on the wrong side of a line the script otherwise draws correctly and discloses at `:145`. Two bounds worth carrying, both **measured by deleting each of the six in turn**, with a pristine control between rows: coverage of the defect is **2 in 6, not 1 in 6** — I recorded 1 on the implementer's first estimate and it was wrong. `run-p05-baselines.ps1` and `verify-gate-of-the-gate.sh` are cited and fail at the citation checker; `check-calibration.py`, `derive-variance-table.py`, `rederive-statistics.py` and **`verify-baselines.sh` itself** all delete green at `PASS (34 checks)`. Reproduced independently here: `:401` extracts names requiring a `scripts/` prefix and yields 6; `:424` extracts citations with **no prefix required** and yields 4, of which `verify-gate-of-the-gate.sh:132` carries no prefix — which is exactly why an estimate made with the naming pattern missed it, rule 43 from the confirming side again. **The sharpest instance is deleting `verify-baselines.sh` from the audited tree**: the gate then reports `document names 6 script(s), 6 present, difference 0` and certifies that the tree ships the gate, while running from the only tree that has one. Note also that the fix has an in-file precedent twenty lines below the defect — `:437` resolves citations with `find "$ROOT/docs/design/lxr-port" …`, correctly rooted at the **audited** tree, which is precisely why the citation checker catches these two deletions and the `$SELF_DIR` checks catch none. And the near-misses that preceded it were rule 54's shape twice over — four uniform `exit=127` runs where WSL could not read a worktree whose `.git` is a file, and an `exit=2` with an empty `root:` that read as gate behaviour but was a PowerShell here-string shipping CRLF into `cd $'/tmp/p05ex\r'`. Discharged against my own apparatus immediately, and it has the identical construct: `store.mjs:6-7` resolves the board with `dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url))` then `join(extensionDirectory, "roadmap.md")` — **structurally `$SELF_DIR`**, so the canvas reads the board beside whichever copy of the extension the host loaded, while my `git diff` and `Get-Content` checks read the copy I edit. Verified safe today for one reason only: exactly **one** copy of `roadmap.md` exists on this machine (`7F6BEBE5EB96`, 64 rules, in this worktree), so the two roots cannot diverge — immunity and defect as one fact for the fourth time, and the fourth is mine. The hazard is dated rather than hypothetical: **this branch is unpushed by design, and the moment it merges the main checkout gains a second copy**, after which any session outside this worktree carries its own board, the canvas renders one and my battery verifies the other, and no contents or extent check I run can tell — subject again. Honest bound on what I established: I proved there is one *candidate*, not that the host loaded it. **That bound is now discharged, and the claim inside it was wrong** — the extension log *does* carry a resolved path, `EXTENSION_PATH=…\kkokosa-fictional-giggle\.github\extensions\lxr-gc-roadmap\extension.mjs`, and since `store.mjs` resolves the board from its own file URL in that same directory, the host demonstrably reads the copy I edit rather than merely the only copy that exists. The subject axis is therefore established by **evidence rather than by uniqueness**, which is what makes it survive the second copy appearing at merge: the standing guard is to read `EXTENSION_PATH` from the log after each reload *and* assert copy-uniqueness, not to rely on either alone. (The count in the parenthetical above is point-in-time; the board carries 67 rules as of this note, and `board-check.ps1` asserts the copy count on every run.) **Fix scope corrected from two sites to three:** `:391` is also wrong-subject and is worse than the other two, so the repair is `:193` and `:407` reading `$BASE/scripts/` *plus* `:391` passing `--lxr-root "$ROOT/docs/design/lxr-port"` — one argument, since the flag already exists at `check-doc-code.py:214`. See rule 68.
64. **Do not correct a claim the other party did not make.** I told the implementer that `verify-baselines.sh` has no `--doc` flag "as a correction to its framing" — true of the script, and it had never claimed otherwise: its `--doc` usage was always about `check-prose-claims.py`, and its fork message named `:288` and `:414` as the document-coupled checks without asserting any flag. I manufactured an error and then corrected it, which costs more than a silent misreading because the other party may accept authorship of a mistake that was never theirs — this one nearly did, declining only because it could not verify its own sent text and refused to accept unverifiable authorship. The check is one line: quote the sentence you are correcting before correcting it, and if you cannot find it, you are arguing with your own paraphrase. The implementer added the reciprocal, which is the stronger half: **a hedge should name what it is hedging.** It declined authorship on *"I cannot verify my own sent text"* when the available claim was *"I did not write it"* — it could not reach the strong ground and settled for the weak without saying so, which reads as a concession and is not one.
65. **When a report carries both a measurement and an inference drawn from it, mark which is which; unmarked, the inference borrows the measurement's standing.** The implementer sent one message containing a paired, controlled demonstration — C1 green and C2 red on the same perturbed tree — and, in the same paragraph and the same voice, the bound *"1 in 6, the other five delete green"*, which was an extrapolation from a grep rather than a measurement. I recorded both into `f98c17684a9` at the demonstration's confidence, and the bound was **wrong: it is 2 in 6**, established afterwards by deleting each of the six. Nothing in the message was false about the demonstration and nothing marked where the evidence stopped. This is rule 57 applied to bounds rather than to batteries — the author selects the extrapolation with the same model that produced the measurement, so it inherits the blind spot while wearing the measurement's authority — and it compounds across sessions, because a coordinator copying a figure onto a durable board strips whatever tentativeness the prose carried. **The reader's guard is the cheaper one: a figure worth writing down is worth asking how it was obtained.**
66. **When a reproduction yields a different number, the first hypothesis is that you reproduced a different thing — not that the original is wrong.** Discharging rule 65 against this board, I re-ran the two gate figures I had recorded but never executed. The subset reproduced exactly. The decoy returned `FAIL (29 passed, 1 failed)` against a recorded `28 passed, 2 failed`, and that correction was one command away from being written down — but my decoy was a renamed *real* checkpoint while the implementer's was fabricated, so mine passed the `schemaVersion` check that theirs failed; a minimal `{}` decoy reproduces `28 passed, 2 failed` exactly. Both runs were correct measurements of different perturbations, and only one of them was a reproduction. **The tell was available before the run: the totals already agreed at 30 checks**, so the disagreement was confined to the split — a property of the decoy, not of the gate — and a discrepancy that leaves the structural figure intact is pointing at the input, not the subject. This is rule 43 from the confirming side, and rule 65 turned on its author: I corrected the implementer for presenting an inference in a measurement's voice, then nearly presented a neighbouring measurement as a refutation, in the same turn.
67. **A checker you retype is a checker whose patterns are unversioned; store the battery beside the artifact and run it.** The standing board battery was retyped from memory on each use, and in one sitting it drifted four times — every drift a false alarm or a blind spot on a healthy board. `^\d+\. \*\*` counted 19 of 66 rules, because the early rules are not bold-prefixed. `^- \*\*[A-Za-z ]+\*\*:` counted 0 of 360 fields, because the colon sits *inside* the bold. A staleness grep matched the very rule that documents the stale figure. And a Status-per-step expectation of 54 was wrong because phases carry a Status too, so the truth is 65 = 54 + 11 — caught on the stored script's first run by an assertion no ad-hoc version had ever bothered to write down. **Then its first draft reproduced rule 59's defect exactly**: rule contiguity derived from the artifact means deleting the highest rule leaves `1..N-1` perfectly contiguous, so the negative control passed a board with a rule removed. Shape can be derived; extent needs a floor stated from outside, raised deliberately. Two general forms, both of which I had already written down and neither of which I applied to my own apparatus: a battery that prints numbers without comparing them cannot fail, and one that derives every expectation from its subject cannot notice the subject shrinking. Lives at `board-check.ps1`, with a paired control as its acceptance evidence.
68. **The author of a demonstration is the worst-placed person to bound its class, because the bound comes from the same search that produced the case.** The implementer's phrasing, offered against itself after its second unmeasured bound in two messages — `1 in 6` when the truth was 2, and *"`:193` and `:407` are simply on the wrong side of a line"* when the truth is three of fourteen. Both bounds arrived attached to demonstrations that held, which is exactly why they were believed. The third site is `:391`, and it is the worst of them: `:193` and `:407` read the audited tree's *document* and test it against the apparatus, whereas `:391` invokes `check-doc-code.py` with no `--lxr-root`, so `:209`-`:211` derive the default from `__file__` and **both sides come from the apparatus** — the audited tree is never opened. That check is the F1 sweep, added because P0.4's gate compared the document to itself and therefore could not catch a document claiming a `calibrate` verb the source lacked; under the positional it compares the document to itself. Verified here rather than taken: all 14 `$SELF_DIR` uses sit at the lines claimed, `:386` `--selftest` is correctly apparatus-rooted because it asserts the checker's own probes fire, and `:326`/`:437` are correctly artifact-rooted. Measured with a `git archive` extract of HEAD and one line appended to the **copy's** `P0.4-harness.md`: unperturbed copy audited from the other checkout gives `PASS (34 checks)` exit 0; **perturbed copy audited from the other checkout also gives `PASS (34 checks)` exit 0**, printing `every one of the 11 harness flags … exists in source` — the apparatus's number, while the tree named in its own banner claims 12; the same perturbed copy audited by its own gate gives `FAIL (33 passed, 1 failed)` with `flag --bogus-flag claimed at P0.4-harness.md:947` and `claimed-but-absent: 12 - 11 present = 1`. That last payload was the implementer's one marked *inference* — it had lost the log — but **my run does not close it**: I perturbed `P0.4-harness.md` and it had perturbed `P0.5-baselines.md`, so mine corroborates the proposition on a different instance rather than settling that run, which it closed itself afterwards. Same verdict is not the same measurement. See rule 71, because the divergence bought something neither of us intended. **the discriminator between blindness and detection is a single digit in a count the gate already prints**, which is rule 26 earning its place.
69. **A destructive command placed in a script "just in case" is the one instrument defect that does not announce itself by producing a wrong number.** The implementer wrote `git -C "$REPO" checkout -- .` as a restore reflex in a throwaway demonstration script, when the edit it meant to undo had been made in the *extract* rather than the repo. It was a no-op purely because the repo had nothing uncommitted; against a dirty tree it would have silently discarded work in the middle of a demonstration, and no line of output would have mentioned it. Every other defect on this board announced itself with a number that came out wrong — 19 of 66, 0 of 360, 11 against 12, `PASS` on a perturbed tree. **This class produces no number at all, so the guard cannot be a comparison:** a throwaway script must not carry a destructive command it does not need, and a restore step belongs where the edit was actually made, named explicitly, never as a blanket over a whole tree. Self-reported by its author after the fact, which is the only route by which this class ever surfaces.
70. **Apparatus deserves the paired control that measurements get.** I claimed everything caught this week lived in a checker rather than in the thing checked. The implementer's boundary is right, and I verified it against git rather than taking it: **13 of the 14 commits on the P0.5 branch touch the document**, with subjects including *correct a false prose claim*, *stop section 7 from restating a gated count the gate already checks*, and *make the harness file counts match what git reports*. The artifact was **not** clean. What held is the **measurements at HEAD**, and the modification counts are exact: 15 of 15 changed paths under `P0.5-baselines/` are in `scripts/`, none is a data file. I then narrowed that to *no re-derivation from the raw CSVs has ever come out different* — **false, and falsified by the document I was auditing, at `:139-141`**: `rederive-statistics.py` found a real defect on its **first** run and moved **331 of 6,600 fields** (F21 — a published p99 of 0.3498 ms where its five invocations mean 0.7668 ms). My evidence could not have witnessed it *in principle*: every data file was added in commit 1 and never modified, so a re-derivation disagreement has no shape in this branch's history, and the fix landed in the working tree before the first commit. That is `:391`'s defect wearing the evidence rather than the checker — both sides of the comparison drawn from one place, so the method decides the answer. The generalisable part is the register: **narrowing a claim feels like the safe direction, so the narrowed version does not get re-tested.** Mine survived one `git log`; the implementer's replacement for it survived one `grep` (rule 72). The forward form is the implementer's, and it is what `board-check.ps1` became: an instrument ships with a paired control demonstrating that it fails on a perturbed input, exactly as a measurement ships with a baseline. An instrument with no control is an untested claim, and every instrument defect found this week surfaced either from someone building a control after the fact or from an author's own confession — never from the instrument itself.
71. **An exact reproduction tests repeatability; a divergent one tests generality — so do not standardise reproductions too hard.** The implementer perturbed `P0.5-baselines.md`; I chose `P0.4-harness.md`, its message having named no file. Neither of us intended a difference, and that difference is the only reason the doc/code sweep's **provenance** was ever tested: two documents, two line numbers — `P0.4-harness.md:947`, one past the end of a 946-line file, and `P0.5-baselines.md:1114`, being 1112 plus a blank and the text, both counts verified here from `git show HEAD:` — each named **correctly**. Run alone, neither result distinguishes correct provenance from *names the first document in its audit list* or from a hardcoded path, because each of us would have seen only our own filename come back and read it as confirmation. — **The second half of that sentence is false, and the implementer falsified it from source.** `check-doc-code.py:228` is `sorted(p for p in lxr.glob("*.md"))`, whose first element is `P0.1-benchmarks.md`; neither run ever returned that name, so *either* run alone already excluded **first-in-list**. The pair excluded only **hardcoded-path**, and a single run perturbing two documents excludes both — which it demonstrated, and which `:130-137` settles without any run at all, since `scan_markdown(doc.read_text(...), doc.name)` passes the origin label in beside the text, making provenance per-document **by construction**. All three verified here. **This is the reciprocal of rule 68:** if the author's search shapes the bound, then a second author's *different* search is worth more than a careful repeat of the first. What survives is the rule's general claim — a divergent reproduction does test generality, and this one tested a property neither of us had thought to specify. What does **not** survive is the necessity: divergence was sufficient, never required, and the coordination corollary I drew from it is retracted in favour of rule 73.

72. **Re-derivation and reading catch disjoint classes of wrong number, and a claim that either is "the only instrument with demonstrated power" is false in both directions.** Correcting rule 70, the implementer wrote that re-derivation from raw data is *the only* instrument in this deliverable that ever caught a defect in a published number. Measured against the committed ledger: **F11, F22 and F24 are all published numbers that are wrong, and re-derivation agrees with every one**, because each is arithmetically correct and wrong in what it *means*. F11's "measured minimum" of exactly 16 MiB for six of ten scenarios is the **search floor**, so every heap factor derived from those six has a denominator that was never measured (`:117-123`). F22's published throughput of **988 op/s** at wks/2.0x is the 1,000 op/s default **arriving successfully**, not capacity (`:154-157`). F24's throughput ratio is **1.000 by construction** — rate-limited by simulated I/O, and it would stay 1.000 for a collector twice as fast (`:549-554`). F21, the one re-derivation did catch, is the exact complement: arithmetic wrong, meaning fine. So the partition is **arithmetic vs meaning**, and this is rule 39's unit problem and rule 42's un-re-derivable claim arriving as measured numbers rather than as prose. — **"Each instrument is blind precisely where the other works" was my own over-reach and the implementer measured it out: that phrasing implies a pair, and there is no second instrument.** Four regimes, not two: F21 **fails the gate**; F22 is **encoded as a fix in code** at four sites (`rederive-statistics.py:85-93` and `:134`'s `phase_of(row["runId"])`, `compare-arm-ratios.py:26`, `compare-sessions.py:32`, `derive-variance-table.py:9-10,48`) so nothing re-checks it; F11 is **detected, printed, and deliberately never failed**; and **F24 has nothing at all** — verified here by a wider sweep than the one that found it, `pinning-heavy-io` appearing in **0** code files across the whole `P0.5-baselines` tree, and none of the 12 registered prose claims touching it. F11's report-don't-fail is the right call and argues its own case at `check-calibration.py:10-14`: failing "would push a future session toward raising the floor until the warning stops, which would replace a true statement with a comfortable one" — the one good argument against making a property an assertion, and it comes with the tension intact, since `:105` detects by `"floor" in note.lower()`, so rewording a note ends detection silently. The clinching detail is at `:163-166`: F22's second consequence is that **the re-derivation script itself carried a silent defect** — it joined published cells to raw rows on `mode`, which for this scenario reads `latency` in *both* phases, so it compared against the mean of ten invocations rather than five. The instrument being nominated as the only one with demonstrated power needed a different instrument to correct it, and the document places F22 first. Marking classes per rule 65: the ledger entries and their contents are **measured**, read from the committed blob; *which* instrument found F11, F22 and F24 is **not stated by the document and I have not established it** — but the structural claim needs no attribution, since re-derivation demonstrably agrees with all three. For P0.6 this is a design constraint, not a scoreboard: a third arm needs both instruments, and `ratioVsBaseline`'s immunity to F21 (it resamples the per-invocation vector, never the published scalar) is the property to preserve when LXR becomes a column.

73. **A free instance is a lottery; a control is N≥2 instances with distinct payloads — brief the control.** This replaces rule 71's coordination corollary, which I had already committed to applying to P0.6's kickoff. The implementer's construction: one extract, two documents perturbed, **one** gate run, `--flag-alpha` into `P0.4-harness.md:948` and `--flag-beta` into `P0.5-baselines.md:1114`, both named correctly, `FAIL (33 passed, 1 failed)`. Same property, deterministic, one session — so precision costs nothing here, and precision is what stops a child inventing its own standard of evidence. **The distinct payloads are load-bearing and worth stating explicitly, because `check-doc-code.py:136` is `found.setdefault(flag, []).extend(sites)`:** sites accumulate under the *flag* key, so two documents perturbed with the **same** flag name merge into one entry with two sites — that still exhibits two filenames, but it cannot detect a **label swap**, the failure where the checker attributes document A's finding to document B. One payload per instance is what turns a two-name result into a checked *pairing*. Two further reasons the control beats the accident, both the implementer's: **an accident cannot be re-run**, so our pair is evidence but not a regression test, whereas a two-document perturbation ships as one — and it should, since `verify-baselines.sh:386`'s `--selftest` asserts the checker's probes fire but nothing asserts they fire at the *right document*. The residue of rule 71 that survives is narrow and worth keeping honest: a free instance can still surface a property **nobody thought to specify**, which is exactly what happened here — but that is a lottery ticket, you cannot schedule a lottery, and a briefing standard must never rest on one. Specify the property, specify at least two instances, let the implementer choose *additional* ones freely.

74. **A control that lands in the blind spot of the check it controls converts an untested assertion into an apparently tested one — so a control must first prove its perturbation is visible to the check's own method.** Rule 73 sent me to audit `board-check.ps1` itself: 12 checks, and until that day controls for 2. Driving each with two distinct payloads found 11 of 12 firing, correctly labelled, with distinguishable output — and exactly one gap, in the **subject** check, which is the one that becomes load-bearing the moment PR #5 merges and creates the second board. Two decoy boards planted in a matching path, and it reported `ok exactly one board on this machine`. The cause, measured rather than reasoned: `Get-ChildItem -Recurse` does not descend into **hidden** directories without `-Force`, `%TEMP%` lives under the hidden `AppData`, and the same tree at the same instant yields **1 copy without `-Force` and 2 with**. So the check had a real blind spot *and* my first control for it landed inside that blind spot. **The dangerous part is the shape of the output**: not an error, but a fluent green sentence that was true of everything the check could see. This is rule 53's dual — 53 says observing only FAIL cannot distinguish *the check fired* from *the harness never reached the document*; the dual is that observing PASS on a perturbed input cannot distinguish *the check correctly passed* from **the perturbation never arrived**. The discipline that follows: a control asserts its own perturbation is detectable by the check's method before it interprets the verdict. Fixed with `-Force`; both payloads now fire and are distinguishable (`2 boards found` vs `3 boards found`), and coverage is now 12 of 12 checks at 2 payloads each. **The check fixed here was itself replaced the same day — see rule 75 — so `-Force` is no longer in the script; the lesson survives the check because it is about controls, not about that check.**

75. **A proxy about to become permanently false for a legitimate reason should be replaced with direct evidence of the property it stood for — not relaxed, and not deleted.** The subject check asserted *exactly one board exists on this machine*. The property it existed to defend is narrower: *the board this script audits is the board the extension host loads*. Uniqueness only ever **implied** that, and merging PR #5 creates a second copy legitimately — so the proxy goes red while the property stays true. Both usual responses to a red check that is not reporting a defect are bad: relax it until it can no longer fire (rule 72's F11 warning — replacing a true statement with a comfortable one), or delete it and lose the axis entirely. A third option existed here only because **the host already writes the answer down**: every extension log carries `EXTENSION_PATH=<dir>\extension.mjs`. Two assertions now replace the one proxy — the **newest** log's directory equals `$PSScriptRoot`, and the number of **distinct** paths across all 59 logs is 1 — and both survive the merge, because two files on disk are fine and two *loaded* boards are not. Six controls at two distinct payloads (rule 73), each printing `perturbation=reached` before its verdict is read (rule 74): fabricated paths `D:\decoy-alpha` / `E:\decoy-beta` fail identity while distinct stays green, and an older decoy beside a correct newest log fails distinct — naming the extra path — while identity stays green, so the two assertions are separately exercised rather than jointly. **The measured side-effect is the stronger argument:** the battery fell from **36 s to 0.37 s**, because the proxy was a recursive scan of all of `C:\` and the direct evidence is a regex over one directory. A battery slow enough to skip is a battery that gets skipped, which is a correctness property and not an ergonomic one. **The condition on this rule is real and should not be dropped:** direct evidence was available because the host happened to record the fact. Where nothing records it, inventing a field to check against is rule 72's `check-calibration.py:103-104` trap — a derived check silently never matches — and the honest move is to state the property as unenforced rather than to enforce a proxy for it. One environment fact worth carrying: the newest log is the **live** one and the host holds it open, so `File.ReadLines` throws on exactly the log carrying the current answer; the read needs an explicit `FileShare::ReadWrite`.

76. **A hazard annotated only at its definition site is undocumented for everyone who consumes the artifact.** `GcTelemetry.cs:233-237` explains, carefully and correctly, that `Gen0Collections` holds the all-generation total and that gen1/gen2 are subsets of it — *"not the gen0-only figure its name suggests."* That annotation is in C# XML doc on a property. What ships is the **name**: `gen0Collections`, in all 144 published rows across three result files, and in `P0.5-baselines.md` at `:541`, `:543`, `:544`, `:550`, with the semantics stated in neither. A P0.6 session reading the JSON key gets a wrong number and no warning, having never opened the file where the warning lives. **The prose is the proof that documentation-at-the-definition-site does not travel:** `:542`'s *"2,042 gen0 against 2,021 gen2 — nearly every collection is a full one, so it is thrashing"* is valid **only** under the subset reading (99%, not the ~50% a literal reading gives), so the author plainly knew — and still wrote "gen0" four times into the artifact a stranger will read. Corroborated: `gen2 > gen0` in **0 of 144 rows**. The discipline: an annotation must sit at the boundary the consumer crosses — the field name, the published schema, the column header — not at the definition, because the consumer's first contact with the concept is the name, and by then the reading is fixed. **The dual matters as much and is the trap I nearly walked into:** a name that *looks* wrong may be right, and renaming the computation rather than the label injects the defect. `MeanPauseMs` divides `GC.GetTotalPauseDuration()` by `Gen0Collections`, which reads like the same unit error and is instead the **correct** denominator — a mean over all pauses needs all collections, exactly as `:271-274` argues — and that fallback branch is **entirely untested** — the whole 1188-line suite builds exactly two `GcSummary` fixtures, `(Observed 20, Gen0 20)` and `(0, 0)`, so nothing exercises it (rule 80). Same misleading name, one place it must be repaired and one place it must be left alone; only reading both settles which is which.

77. **Evidence that a check *mentioned* your input is not evidence that it *consumed* your input.** Rule 74 says a control must prove its perturbation is visible to the check's method. My first implementation of that proof asserted the fabricated log directory appeared somewhere in the battery's output — and it reported `reached` on all 27 cases while **every fabricated log was invisible**, because the battery selects with `-Filter '*lxr-gc-roadmap*.log'` and I had named them `ext-1.log`. The path appeared in the output for the worst possible reason: it is quoted in the message *"no extension log under '…'"* that reports them missing. A presence test on the input's name is satisfied by the error that says the input was absent. The repaired form asserts the **consumption signature** instead — no case may emit `no extension log` — which is a statement about what the check did with the payload rather than about what it printed. **The second instance the same run produced, and it is the same error in the other direction:** the "correct path" payload was built locally from `$env:TEMP`, which yields the 8.3 short form `KONRAD~1`, while the battery's `$PSScriptRoot` resolves long — so identity failed on all 27 cases *including pristine*, and a control that fails everywhere is as uninformative as one that passes everywhere. The fix was to stop reconstructing the value and **ask the instrument for it**: the battery prints `self :` in its banner, so the control now takes the check's own answer and no normalization rule has to be kept in sync. Both defects are one shape — the control and the check disagreed about what the input *was*, and in neither case did the disagreement announce itself as an error.

78. **A universal that quantifies over another party's evidence is unfalsifiable by its author — and this one was contradicted by a finding that author had produced himself.** The implementer wrote *"every defect either of us has produced since PR #5 opened is in apparatus"*, a claim about **my** commits. I justified this as unfalsifiable-by-its-author on the grounds that the implementer could not reach my branch — **that justification is false and the implementer disproved it.** Linked worktrees share one object database (`--git-common-dir` is `C:/github/runtime-fork/.git` for both), so every board commit, including ones made minutes earlier, is readable from its checkout by `git cat-file`. Unpushed means unreachable from another *clone*, and we are not in another clone. The case is therefore the same shape as the other four — reachable by both parties, checked by neither — and the "new variant" claim is withdrawn. What survives is the discipline, on its own merits: state the scope you can inspect. Measured: `c5ff8b90988` (15:00, PR #5 opened 08:18) committed rule 70 asserting *"no re-derivation from the raw CSVs has ever come out different"*, and `133418924af` corrected it 13 minutes later. That is a defect in the artifact, inside the stated window, and it sits on the **measurements** side of the implementer's own partition — it is a statement about what re-derivation runs have shown, not about apparatus. **The falsifying evidence was the implementer's own catch**, delivered two exchanges earlier: `P0.5-baselines.md:139-141`, `rederive-statistics.py` failing on its first run. So the claim was not merely unverified by its author; it was refuted by something the author personally found and could not connect, because connecting it required reading a history he has no access to. The discipline: state the scope you can inspect, and let the other party answer for theirs — a shared universal needs both halves measured, and only one of us can measure each. **A tooling fact that nearly hid this:** `git log -S<phrase>` reports commits where the *occurrence count* changes, so a correction that **retains the false sentence as a quotation** — which is exactly how a retraction should be written — is invisible to it. `-S` returned 1 commit and `-G`, which searches the diff text, returned 2. Searching for a retracted claim with `-S` finds the assertion and hides the retraction.

79. **Widening another party's finding needs the same standard of evidence the finding itself did — a data signature is not a class.** The implementer declined to bound F24's class (its rule 68), so I tried to, from a signature I could compute in one pass over the per-invocation CSV: throughput spread under 10% while collection counts vary several-fold. Four of ten scenarios matched, and I was one commit from filing a blocker four times the size of the one I was verifying. **Three of the four are correct by design.** `aspnet-request-load` already carries `Primary = PrimaryMetric.Latency` in `ScenarioCatalog.cs` — F24's own prescribed fix, already applied, which the signature cannot see. `low-allocation-compute` and `pointer-chasing` record zero collections in every valid row because they are a deliberate paired barrier experiment: the first isolates the write barrier LXR pays on every reference store "regardless of how much garbage there is to reclaim", the second is its high-store partner so that "the pair separates per-store barrier cost from per-object cost". Under the signature alone I would have declared the two most carefully justified scenarios in the catalog vacuous — including the one the harness uses as its own resolution test — on the grounds that the collector never ran, which is the entire point of them. What separated the real case from the three false ones was a **declaration**: a metric enum and a rationale, both in code I had not read, neither recoverable from the numbers. Two consequences. **For the finding:** the class is exactly one **in the throughput phase, which is the only phase this signature was computed over** — a scope I failed to state and which rule 83 shows is load-bearing, because the same property holds for nine of ten scenarios in the latency phase. The gate that bounds it must read declarations rather than infer intent from data. **For the method:** this is rule 76's dual arriving from the other side — there a *name* looked wrong and the number was right, here the *numbers* looked wrong and the design was right. Before escalating a peer's finding, read the thing that says why the code is the way it is. Cost of the discipline: four commands. Cost of skipping it: a false blocker in the next step's kickoff, aimed at the harness's precision instrument.

80. **A published quotient whose inputs are unpublished cannot be re-derived, and the gate quietly downgrades it to a copy check — `pauseAverageMs` is that field, and I republished an inference about it as fact.** The implementer reported that `MeanPauseMs`'s untested fallback is "live in 8 of 144 rows", marking the branch-to-`pauseSource` mapping as an inference corroborated by the partition being exact with no residue. I carried it into two places on this board **without the marking**, which is rule 65 failing at the receiving end: a peer's marked inference becomes an unmarked fact the moment it is restated. Measured, the inference does not hold and the corroboration cannot bear on it. `GcTelemetry.cs:195` makes `distributionTrusted` false in **two disjoint ways** — `pauses.Length == 0`, which reaches the untested fallback, or `pauses.Length > 0 && shortfall > 2`, which reaches the *tested* suspensions branch — and both emit the same `total-pause-duration-only` label and both suppress the percentiles, which is exactly what the 8 rows show (`withP99=0, withAvg=8`). The partition being exact is true by construction of the ternary chain at `:207-215` and discriminates nothing. **It is undecidable from the artifacts**: 55 published keys per row include `pauseAverageMs` and `pauseSource` but neither `totalPauseMs` nor `observedPauseCount` nor `pauseShortfall` — the label is published and its inputs are not. Two consequences worth more than the original claim. **The gate cannot see this field's value:** `rederive-statistics.py:52` classes `pauseAverageMs` as a `COPY_FIELD`, so re-derivation checks the published scalar equals an invocation's scalar and never touches the quotient — the one instrument with demonstrated power is structurally blind to how the number was computed, for want of a denominator. **And what needs no inference at all is the real finding:** the fallback branch has no fixture anywhere in the 1188-line suite, which builds exactly two `GcSummary` values, `(20, 20)` and `(0, 0)`. So P0.6 owes two things, not one — add the missing fixture, asserting the denominator is the all-generation count against *both* misreadings (`TotalPauseMs / (20-19)`, the gen0-only "correction" rule 76 warns about, and `TotalPauseMs / 41`, the triple-count the existing test already guards); and **publish the denominator**, which promotes the field from copy to derived, makes the branch decidable by one grep, and would have prevented the implementer's own near-miss from a defaulted `r.get("totalPauseMs", 0)` reading a key that exists in none of the 144 rows.

81. **An audit that searches one location for items that legitimately live in several reports absence as a defect — and acting on that verdict would have duplicated a claim, which is the hazard rule 63 exists for.** Auditing whether everything I had told the user P0.6 "carries" is actually retrievable from the board, I grepped the P0.6 `Open` field for eleven carry-forward items. Two came back `ABSENT`. One was real: rule 80's *publish the denominator* deliverable existed only inside the rule, never in the field an implementer reads — precisely the F24 shape I had just endorsed, an assignment written where nothing points at it, and it is now carried into `Open` with its two concrete assertions. **The other was my checker's fault:** `large-object-pressure` is absent from `Open` because the inversion lives in P0.6's `Correctness` field, which is its correct home. Had I trusted the verdict I would have copied it into `Open`, producing two statements of one finding that can drift apart — rule 63's two-subject hazard, manufactured by a control built to prevent omissions. The general form: **a single plausible `ABSENT` is more dangerous than a control that fails everywhere**, because rule 77's all-red case is obviously broken while one red item looks like a finding and invites a fix. Scope the search to where the property may legitimately live, which for a step means every field of that step, not the field the auditor happens to have in hand. A second-order note worth keeping: the same pass produced a **false positive** in the other direction when `[regex]::Match` returned `Success=false` with `Index=0`, and printing context around index 0 showed the field's opening sentence as though it were a hit — a not-found result rendered as a plausible excerpt, which is rule 74 in a formatting helper.

82. **Every over-reach in this run was a universal quantified over history, and history is the one subject with no standing instrument.** The implementer's observation, and it is the durable output of the whole exchange: across five corrections on both sides, *not one* of the false claims was about a measurement or about code. They were `everything`, `only`, `never`, `nowhere else`, `first`, `each` — assertions about the record. A measurement can be re-measured and code can be read, so a wrong claim about either meets an instrument built to meet it; `rederive-statistics.py` catches an arithmetic defect and reading catches a semantic one. A claim about what has happened has nothing pointed at it, and both parties kept shipping them at exactly the rate the absence predicts. **Two things this replaces.** My rule 78 justified its discipline on the claim being unfalsifiable by its author, and that was wrong: linked worktrees share one object database, so the board was always one `git cat-file` away from the implementer, and its own commits were always one away from me. Reachable by both, checked by neither — which is the *same* shape as the other four, not a variant. **And the implementer's counterexample beats mine on its own terms.** `669a3dba027` (author 11:04:09, forty-six minutes after PR #5 opened at 10:18:27 local) put two false claims into `P0.5-baselines.md` itself — *"Its minimum is 4 MiB where Server needs 35–43"*, which the document now records at `:431` as previously-read-and-wrong, and *"odd or leaves a remainder"* as the mechanism defeating exact ×1.3, true but naming the wrong cause since 36 is even and 36 × 1.3 = 46.8 still fails — corrected 39 and 55 minutes later. That falsifies *"every defect either of us has produced is in apparatus"* under **both** readings, with no argument about categories, because it is in the deliverable. My counterexample needed the argument, since `133418924af` repaired rule 70 while touching **zero bytes** of the deliverable. **And the argument itself was ill-formed**, which is the sharpest thing either of us said: apparatus-versus-artifact is a **role, not a location**. `roadmap.md` is artifact to `board-check.ps1` and apparatus to P0.5, and it changes side with the question being asked, so a claim using that partition must name the deliverable or it silently means two things. What to do about it, since no instrument is coming: when a sentence quantifies over the record, either bound it to what a named command over a named range returns, or do not write it. The `-S`/`-G` fact from 78 survives intact and was independently reproduced from the shared object store.

83. **The defect F24 names is nine times larger than F24 states, it is in the committed matrix, and both of us bounded it to one scenario by measuring only the phase where the bound holds.** The implementer proposed flipping `pinning-heavy-io` to `Primary = Latency` and I verified every number behind it — all reproduce exactly: `latencyP99Ms` 0.31714/0.29814, 0.2674/0.20448, 0.19778/0.17312 give srv/wks of 0.940, 0.765, 0.875 while `ratioVsBaseline` publishes 0.999998, 0.999999, 0.99999 on those same rows, with `operationsPerSecond` pinned at 21,481.6. `Primary` is genuinely consumed, at **four** sites rather than the three it named — `Aggregator.cs:112` picks the field, `:159` names the statistic, `MatrixRunner.cs:204` forces the mode, and `Reaggregator.cs:213` is the fourth, the one that makes its own no-re-run path possible. **Then following it generalised the finding past both our bounds.** Measured over the 68 valid wks/srv latency-phase rows in the three committed result files: **nine of ten scenarios publish a latency-phase ratio within 0.16% of 1.000**, and the sole exception is `aspnet-request-load` at 12.80% — the only scenario in the catalog declared `Primary = Latency`. The correspondence is exact and the mechanism is documented at `Lxr.Harness.Runner/Program.cs:200`: latency-phase arrival rates are *fixed from a prior throughput pass*, so `operationsPerSecond` is pinned by construction for every arm, and `Aggregator.cs:112` reads exactly that field for all nine Throughput-primary scenarios. F24 is not a fact about one scenario's I/O rate; it is a fact about **choosing the ratio basis per scenario when what is measurable is a property of the phase**. **This changes the fix.** The flip repairs one of nine and costs something — `MatrixRunner:204` would force `mode=latency` in both phases, the F22 shape, safe today only because all four consumers join on `runId` and unsafe the moment a P0.6 tool joins on `mode`. Making the basis a function of **(scenario, phase)** repairs all nine, touches no catalogue row, leaves `Primary` and therefore `:204` alone, and needs **no re-run at all**: `latencyP99Ms` is populated in **68 of 68** latency-phase rows of the published JSON, against **0 of 69** in the throughput phase for every scenario except `aspnet-request-load`.
