One decision it forces rather than settles, and P0.6 must take it deliberately: `aspnet-request-load` is the single row where a phase-dependent basis changes a currently informative number, because its throughput-phase ratio of 1.1305 is computed on latency today. **And the scope lesson is rule 82 arriving one message later, in the artifact rather than the prose.** My rule 79 bound F24 to one scenario of ten from a throughput-phase signature and stated it without naming the phase; the implementer bound it to one scenario from latency-phase P99s and also stated it unscoped. Both bounds are true of the phase measured and false of the matrix. Neither of us wrote a universal about history this time — we wrote one about **data**, and it failed the same way, because the quantifier ranged over a set neither of us had enumerated. **And the first draft of this rule committed the error it names.** It published *"0 of 6 throughput-phase rows"* for the scenarios lacking `latencyP99Ms`; 6 is `pinning-heavy-io`'s own row count, and the figure over the set actually claimed is **0 of 69**. Enumerating afterwards, which is what I had not done: three result files and no other `p0-5` result JSON in the tree, `collector` taking only `wks` and `srv`, **143 of 144 rows valid** with the single exclusion being `lifecycle-semantics/wks/1.3` at `status=crashed` — in the *throughput* phase, so the latency-phase figures are untouched by it and `68 of 68` and `nine of ten` both stand. Naming a failure mode does not confer immunity to it, and the interval between naming and repeating it was one commit. The operational form is therefore not *"remember the scope"* but the mechanical one: **before a count ships, print the denominator of the set it ranges over and check it is not the denominator of the case that suggested it.** **A second self-caught over-reach in the same hour, of a different shape and worth separating:** carrying the four `Primary` consumers into P0.6 I wrote that changing `Aggregator.cs:112` without `Reaggregator.cs:213` would make re-aggregated output diverge from a fresh run. False — `:213` reconstructs a cell and **delegates** to the same `Aggregator` at `:96`, `:97` and `:127`, so the fix propagates for free. I had inferred an independent decision path from a symbol match, `Primary = ScenarioCatalog.Get(...)`, without reading what the file does with it. Reading it produced the better finding, now in the directive: `:213` needs no change but the design does, because a phase-keyed basis needs a phase *on the cell* and neither `MatrixCell` nor `RunResult` has one — `RunId` lives on `RunnerOptions.cs:55` and reaches the artifact only as free text in `notes` via `Aggregator.cs:368`. **The denominator error came from not enumerating a set; this one came from not opening a file**, and only the first is caught by printing denominators. A grep hit locates a symbol and says nothing about the control flow around it.

84. **"Name the deliverable" is not advice about wording; it is the failure mode itself, and this run produced three instances in one hour.** Rule 82 recorded the implementer's point that apparatus-versus-artifact is a role rather than a location. The sharper fact is that *artifact* was already ambiguous inside a single step, because P0.5 publishes **two** files with overlapping column names and different contracts: the JSON result rows and the per-invocation CSV at `Publisher.cs:36-41`. `pauseAverageMs`, `gen0Collections` and the pause percentiles appear in both. Three claims failed on exactly that. **Mine, first:** P0.6's rule-80 deliverable said to publish `observedPauseCount` and `totalPauseMs` *"beside `pauseAverageMs` in the result rows"*, which names the JSON — but `rederive-statistics.py` takes both files (`:112-113`) and the quotient is formed **per invocation**, so the CSV is where the inputs have to land for the gate to evaluate the switch. **Mine, second:** carrying the phase precondition I wrote that the run id reaches "the artifact" only as free text in `notes`; the CSV has `runId` and `mode` as first-class columns (`Publisher.cs:37`), which is precisely why `rederive-statistics.py:134` can call `phase_of(row["runId"])`. True of the JSON, false of the CSV, and the gap is one artifact wide rather than two. **The implementer's, and it is the mildest:** that a JSON-only change leaves the instrument *"exactly as blind as it is now"* — too strong, since publishing all three fields in one row permits an intra-row arithmetic check that does not exist today. Weaker than the CSV fix, not equal to nothing. Its recommendation is right and improves the item twice over: put the fields in the CSV, and then **`pauseSource` becomes derivable rather than copied**, retiring a `COPY_FIELD` instead of adding two. **And the contract was written down the whole time.** `Publisher.cs:33-34` says the CSV's columns *"are the exact vector the bootstrap resamples, so a reader can recompute the published mean and re-run the interval without the harness."* `pauseAverageMs` sits in that header at `:39` and is the column the promise fails for — a quotient whose numerator and denominator are both absent from the file that promises recomputability. That is the third time this run that the sentence bounding a finding was in a file adjacent to the numbers and unread: the catalogue docstrings for rule 79, `:553` for the implementer, this for both of us. **Operational form:** when a field name appears in more than one published file, a claim or a deliverable naming that field is ill-formed until it names the file, and the check is mechanical — grep the name across the emitters before writing the sentence. **Measured afterwards, the surface is most of the schema:** of the CSV's 36 columns, **33 appear in the JSON rows too**; only `runId`, `mode` and `invocation` are CSV-only, and 22 keys are JSON-only, among them every `ratio*` field and `pauseSource`. So the ambiguous case is the default and the unambiguous one is the exception — which is why treating this as a wording nicety was wrong. Sweeping P0.6's directive under that rule found no further false claims but one weak one, now fixed: *"needs no re-run"* rested on `latencyP99Ms` being **68 of 68** in the published JSON, when `Aggregator.TryReadPrimary` reads the field from an invocation's **report**. The per-invocation CSV settles it properly at **340 of 340** latency-phase against **30 of 359** throughput-phase, and the entry now carries both. A projection agreeing with its source is evidence; a projection *standing in for* its source is the same error at one remove. **The same ambiguity governs file citations, and there it resolves to plausible wrong content rather than to an error.** Measured over the board's 60 `file:line` citations at the reviewed tree: 18 name a file that matches more than one path. `Program.cs` matches **four** files under the harness alone and 217 across the repository, and **two of the four have a line 200** — the Runner's is the arrival-rate mechanism, the Tests' is unrelated but readable — so the reader who resolves it wrongly gets something that looks like an answer. `Aggregator.cs` collides with `System.Diagnostics.DiagnosticSource`'s own aggregator, which is worse than a random collision because the wrong file is also about aggregation. P0.6's entry now declares its citation root. **And the sweep that measured this is the reason no citation checker was built.** A naive one flags 4 of the 60 as out of range — `P0.4-harness.md:947`/`:948` past a 946-line file and `P0.5-baselines.md:1114` past a 1112-line one. All four are correct: they cite lines a perturbation control *appended*, and the board says so in the sentence beside them, having verified both counts from `git show` when it wrote them. A checker with a 6.7% false-alarm rate on a healthy board is one that gets ignored, and an ignored checker is worse than none — which is the failure `board-check.ps1`'s own header already records, a staleness grep matching the very rule that documented the stale figure. The line-number claims are pinned to an immutable ref and cannot rot; **what needed fixing was the ambiguity, not the arithmetic**, and that took an edit rather than an instrument. **One more instance, from the sweep itself.** My first pass read the directive by line index, which rule 84's own insertion had shifted by one, and reported **zero** ambiguous field names in it — a clean bill of health produced by scanning a different line. That is rule 74 inside the audit meant to enforce rule 84: a non-arrival returning a plausible verdict, and the plausible verdict here was *pass*. The standing convention to locate board fields by content rather than index exists for edits; it applies identically to reads, and a sweep that finds nothing should be the most suspected result, not the most reassuring. **Fourth axis, and the sharpest form the rule takes: two different quantities landing on the same integer in one document.** P0.5's session reported that `inducedCollections` is constant across **699 valid invocations** and, in the same message, that the ratio directive yields 699 well-formed pairs — the first a count of CSV rows, the second a count of (cell, column) pairs, and the second serving as the denominator of a derived false-positive estimate. **The collision was manufactured by a keying defect, which is the sharpest thing this axis has to say.** Under the design key that rule 91 later forced, the second quantity is **812 well-formed pairs**; the shared integer existed only while the key pooled all three sessions into single arms of 10 and 13, and a coincidence produced by a defect is worse than an ordinary one because it reads as corroboration — the figure that was wrong is the one the agreement made look checked. The first figure is correct, the second was a different quantity computed over a population that was never run; nothing in either sentence distinguishes them, and a reader checking the arithmetic has no way to know which 699 the estimate divides. Naming the artifact does not help here, because both derive from the same artifact — what disambiguates is naming the *unit being counted*. So the rule's operational form gains a third clause: name the artifact, name the estimator, and name what the integer counts. **A further axis arrived from the same session one round later, earned against a table of mine.** I published a comparison for `pinning-heavy-io` / `pauseP99Ms` naming the heap factor, the ratio, the p-value and the separation — and not the phase. Both phases carry 5+5 at every heap for that scenario and column, so both produce a complete, individually plausible table, and they do not agree: throughput gives ratios **4.05 / 4.70 / 2.61** at one-sided p of **1, 1, 2 of 252**, while latency gives **1.50 / 1.23 / 1.03** at **1, 1, 87 of 252**. At 6.0x the throughput reading is 2 of 252 and the latency reading is 87 of 252 — indistinguishable from null. **A reader who checks a phase-free table against the wrong phase gets numbers that are each plausible and a conclusion that inverts at the top of the heap ladder**, which is worse than the other three axes, because those produce a figure that looks wrong to someone who knows the artifact. So: **name the slice.** (This board already spent the ordinal “fourth axis” on the unit clause at `5d3246b1163`, so the axis is named rather than numbered here; the P0.5 session counts it fourth and the disagreement is about counting, not content.) — **Measured, and it retires the item's stated precondition: `pauseSource`'s load-bearing value is derivable from the CSV *as it stands today*.** Rule 84 concluded that moving the fields into the CSV would make `pauseSource` derivable rather than copied. It is already derivable. Over the union of all three invocation CSVs — **699 valid rows** (s2 595 + s3 80 + s4sdk 24), 36 columns — the predicate “`pauseAverageMs` parses numeric **and** `pauseP99Ms` is blank” selects exactly **25 rows**, because a total pause duration without individual samples *is* `total-pause-duration-only (event stream incomplete)`: the numerator survives, the percentile cannot. Those 25 are **set-identical** to the 25 selected by the disjoint criterion “blank `pauseP99Ms` with `gen0Collections > 0`”, group for group — `cyclic-garbage`/wks/throughput 9 rows at 132,257 collections, srv/throughput 8 at 89,045, `multi-thread-throughput`/wks/throughput 3 at 9,846, `cyclic-garbage`/srv/latency 2 at 15,097, wks/latency 2 at 13,894, `multi-thread-throughput`/srv/throughput 1 at 2,949 — two predicates over non-overlapping columns returning one row set. **The derived signal is strictly better than the label it would replace.** Those 25 rows span **10** distinct (scenario, collector, mode, heapFactor) cells, while a census of all three JSON artifacts finds only **8** `total-pause-duration-only` labels (8 in s2, **0** in s3 and s4sdk, matching the signature's own s2-only distribution), because the label is emitted under `ValidOutcomes[^1]` — last invocation only. The derived predicate is per-row and complete; the label under-reports by two cells. The same census independently settles the tally: 78 + 21 + 12 + 8 = **119** labels plus one `None`, the crashed `lifecycle-semantics`/wks/1.3 row. So the P0.6 item is real and its **precondition is false** — publishing the fields buys *diagnosis*, not *detection*, and a gate over today's artifact can already flag every damaged row. The bound that hid this is also false by cardinality: of 36 columns only **12** parse numeric in all 699 rows (six of them configuration or identity — `heapFactor`, `heapLimitMb`, `invocation`, `warmupSeconds`, `steadyStateSeconds`, `seed`), 26 parse numeric in at least one, and **14 are numeric in some rows and blank in others** — the ten latency/rate columns at 329 blanks each, `committedMb` 101, `pauseAverageMs` 131, `pauseP99Ms` and `pauseMaxMs` 156. **A field the artifact lacks is not the same as information the artifact lacks; look for a derivable proxy before ranking a schema change as a blocker, because “the column is missing” is a statement about the header and “the signal is missing” is a statement about the data.**
85. **A guard against a check matching *nothing* is not a guard against it matching *fewer things than before*.** `board-claims-check.ps1` was written with rule 74 in mind: a pattern that locates no sentence fails loudly, because a reworded claim otherwise retires its own check in silence. Its coverage control then found the case the guard does not cover. Perturbing **nine of ten** to **three of ten** moved that site outside its own closed alternation `(nine|\d+)`, so the pattern matched **one** site instead of two, the surviving site was the uncorrupted one, and the checker printed `1 occurrence(s), all agree` at exit 0 over a board that had just been falsified. Non-arrival was the failure mode I had guarded; **partial** arrival is the one that got through, and no non-empty test can see it, because the population that shrank is the population being counted. Two fixes, and the second is the general one: widen the pattern so corruption stays inside it *and is then rejected* rather than falling out of scope, and **declare how many sites each claim occupies**, so a site leaving is arithmetic rather than inference. The site count is the one number in that file not derived from the artifacts — it is a property of how often the board chooses to state a fact — which is exactly why it needs its own control, and each site is now proved individually load-bearing by removing it alone. The general form for anything that verifies by search: **a search-based check must assert its own hit count, or a claim can be deleted from under it without changing the verdict.** **That general form applies one level up, to the sweep itself, and today it caught me there.** The coverage sweep does not restate the claim patterns — it *extracts* them from the checker's source with `re\s+= (?:'(?<r1>[^']*)'|"(?<r2>[^"]*)")`, which makes it a search-based check over PowerShell source, and rule 85 therefore binds it. It obeys: it asserts that the number of claims the checker **reports** equals the number it can **extract**. Adding four rule 50 claims, the checker printed `PASS (58)` with every claim `ok` and every negative control firing, and the sweep returned `FAIL — unperturbed board passes but reports 58 claims where 57 were extracted`. **One claim was passing and invisible to the instrument that adversarially tests claims**, and in every other output it was indistinguishable from a healthy one. The missing claim's pattern contains `grep -c '^RESULT: PASS'`, and the extractor delimits on `'`: **the delimiter a parser splits on is exactly the character a pattern about quoted text has to contain, so the claim least visible to the check is the one whose subject is quoting.** The wider lesson is about layers rather than about apostrophes. The same twenty characters had to be written three ways and each layer failed once, each caught by a different instrument and **none of them able to see the other two**: a PowerShell double-quoted string treats the backtick as an escape character, so the first attempt died in the **parser**; a single-quoted string spells one apostrophe by doubling it, I wrote four, and the pattern matched nothing, caught **in place by the checker**; and the extractor's negated-character-class branch cannot span a doubled apostrophe at all, caught **only by the sweep's count invariant.** Escaping a delimiter correctly through three conventions is three chances to be wrong and no chance to be told. The fix is not a fourth escaping — it is `\x27`, which removes the character from every layer at once and leaves the recovered pattern matching `177` exactly as before. **Prefer eliminating a delimiter over escaping it, and when an instrument parses another instrument's source, the count invariant is not bookkeeping — it is the only thing standing between a green run and a check nobody is testing.** *Written out, this paragraph then broke the board's own two delimiter checks — `rules with unbalanced backticks: 1` and `doubled apostrophes: 1` — because stating the defect precisely required quoting the two characters the gate counts. Fourth and fifth layers, caught by a fourth instrument, and the fix was the same one: say the character's name instead of spelling it. It then took two rounds, because clearing the first doubled apostrophe left a second one standing elsewhere in the same paragraph — so even the repair for a rule about fixing the class was made one instance at a time.* **A fourth layer surfaced while gating rule 107’s instance, and it is the one that will recur, because this board’s prose uses the character everywhere.** PowerShell accepts the Unicode right single quotation mark **U+2019** as a string delimiter, exactly as if it were an ASCII apostrophe — so a single-quoted pattern containing the typographic apostrophe this board writes by default terminates early, and the file dies at parse time with `Unexpected token`. Neither existing detector can see it: the gate’s doubled-apostrophe check counts `'` and this character is not that, and the sweep’s extractor scans for the same ASCII delimiter. The repair is the shape already established here — write `\u2019` and let .NET’s regex engine resolve it, removing the character from the PowerShell layer entirely instead of escaping it there.

86. **When coverage is missing because a *selector* picks one item, enlarging the set it picks from relocates the gap rather than closing it.** The measured case: `pinning-heavy-io`'s pause differs by 6.98x srv/wks on rows publishing a ratio of 0.9999, and the proposed repair was a third member for `PrimaryMetric`. But a selector returns one field per row whatever its domain, so a pause basis would have bought the pause ratio by giving up the throughput ratio — and the throughput ratio is not noise there, it is the finding that the I/O limiter binds. The tell is that the answer to "why does X have no statistics?" was "X is not selectable", which invites widening the domain; the real answer is that **selection was the wrong operation** and statistics should be computed for every comparable column, with the selector demoted to choosing which result leads. Two distinct questions had been conflated in one field — which measurement is this scenario's headline, and which columns deserve a confidence interval — and no value of the first can answer the second. Before accepting a proposal that adds a member to an enum, a variant to a mode, or a case to a switch, state which existing case now goes uncovered; if the honest answer is "one of the ones that was covered", the fix is one level up. A second instance, in a different instrument and reached by a different route: section 6.4's variance table omits `pauseP99Ms` because `derive-variance-table.py:28` is `PHASE_METRIC = {"throughput": "operationsPerSecond", "latency": "latencyP99Ms"}` — one metric per phase — so a column that is no phase's designated metric can never receive a row, and adding a third phase would not help, because pause is not a phase. Two instruments, two selectors, the same gap, neither closable by widening a domain.

87. **A derived figure that reproduces no published figure is a guess however close it lands, and near-agreement between two such guesses is not corroboration.** Two independent derivations of the same *absent* table row landed at 94 cells / median 8.52% and 96 cells / median 8.37%, agreeing exactly on `48` cells above the floor and on a `180.27%` maximum; agreement on the extrema made both look sound and neither was checkable. What settled it was reproducing first the two rows the document already publishes — `operationsPerSecond` 59 / 1.60% / 5.82% / 0 of 59 and `latencyP99Ms` 60 / 11.67% / 187.07% / 34 of 60 — which failed on the first attempt and named its own cause: `derive-variance-table.py` takes **one** CSV (`load_cells(args.csv)`), and unioning the three session CSVs charges cross-session drift to within-cell variance. The partition was right and the population was wrong, so the *cell counts* came out exactly right (59, 60) while every statistic was inflated (median 1.79%, max 13.27%, 3 above the floor instead of 0). **Cell counts agreeing is evidence about the partition and none whatever about the population.** Reproduce the published rows exactly before publishing a new one, and read a failed control as a statement about your derivation rather than about the document.

88. **Before building a checker for a class of error, run its predicate against the artifact when it is *healthy* and count the false alarms — a predicate that sounds exact can fire on most of what it is meant to bless.** Two candidate instruments for cross-artifact citation correctness were killed this way, both proposed as exact and both measured before any code was written. *Citations must carry a verbatim fragment of what they cite*: across the eight `rule N` citations in P0.5's deliverable, independently verified as **4 of 4 distinct rules correct**, only **2 of 8** carry a 5-or-more word verbatim run — the predicate flags six correct citations, a 75% false-alarm rate on a document with no citation defects at all. *A cited identifier must be stable, so a rule's text may gain sentences but never be replaced*: across the **100** commits touching this board up to `a4eb4dbaedb`, **22** edits extend a rule and **25** replace text in place, because correcting a rule where it stands is rule 22 operating as designed. The pin is not decoration and was not there when this was first written: the very next board commit, `5d3246b1163`, appended rule 84's fourth axis in place and moved the extension count to 23, so a sentence that was exactly true when committed was false one commit later — see rule 90. The second measurement also refuted the estimate that motivated it — the scan was written expecting a single violation, and its hardcoded closing line asserting "the one real identity change" shipped in the same output as the twenty-five that contradict it. What survives is the decidable residue, which is one line: **every cited rule number must exist**, currently 0 dangling across both documents. The rest is discipline — resolve the text out of the shared object store and quote it when the claim leans on it — and that discipline caught a real miscitation this week where neither checker would have. — **And the rate is predictable before you measure it, from the index's density in the range being searched.** The implementer's F38 prose-figure checker scans only comma-formatted integers (≥ 1,000). That reads as a stylistic scope choice; it is in fact the threshold at which the check's evidence becomes valid. Measured against P0.5's deliverable and its three invocation CSVs (**1,041** distinct invocation values, **377** cell means): as written the scan extracts **24** prose figures and reports **0** single-invocation leaks. Widening the *same* predicate to bare sub-1,000 integers extracts **696** figures and reports **74** leaks over 24 distinct values — and every one is spurious: `16 MiB` the search floor, `128 MiB` a heap limit, `166 probes`, `474 preserved result files`, `99 MiB` a heap minimum, and `72` matched from inside a SHA-256 digest. A **100%** false-alarm rate, worse than the 75% that killed the verbatim-fragment predicate above. **The cause is not loose writing but index occupancy:** of the integers in [1, 1000) the invocation index holds **275 of 999 — 27.5%** — against **2.8%** in [1000, 10000) and **0.04%** above 10,000. When a quarter of the value range sits in the index, exact equality is not evidence; coincidence is the expected outcome. The predicate never changed and its precision fell to zero purely by moving the range it searches. **Before widening a matcher's scope, compute what fraction of the new range the index already occupies — precision is a property of the index rather than of the predicate, and a scope restriction that looks like fussiness is often the whole reason the check works.**

89. **Before adopting a threshold, compute the best value the design can attain and check that the threshold lies inside it — a claim can be *unreachable* rather than merely unlikely, and no amount of data rescues it.** The exact one-sided permutation test at five invocations against five enumerates `C(10,5) = 252` arrangements, so the smallest attainable p is **1/252 = 0.003968** and the largest usable one is 12/252 = 0.047619. Bonferroni over an interpreted family of size *m* demands p ≤ 0.05/m: at **m = 12** that is 4.1667e-3 and the floor clears it; at **m = 13** it is 3.8462e-3 and the floor does not. So **twelve is the largest interpreted family in which any cell of this design can be called significant** — above it, a cell whose arms separate completely, with every one of the 251 other arrangements less extreme than the observed one, still fails correction. Rule 86's "significance for every comparable column" over 693 well-formed pairs would need 7.2150e-5, which is **55** times below the floor: the directive is not noisy at n=5, it is **unattainable**, and that is a property of the design rather than of the measurements. Two escapes exist and both are design changes rather than analysis choices — hold the interpreted family at or below twelve, or raise n, since `C(12,6) = 924` moves the floor to 1.0823e-3 and the budget to **46**. This is the dual of rule 88 and the pair should be read together: there a predicate fired on artifacts that were healthy, here a predicate cannot fire at all, and both failures are invisible until the predicate is evaluated against the *design* rather than argued from its wording.

90. **A measurement over a population that your own commit joins must be pinned to a hash in the same sentence, or it is false as soon as you write it down.** The rule-88 figures — 100 commits touching this board, 22 extensions, 25 in-place replacements — were exact when committed at `a4eb4dbaedb`. The commit that *stated* them left them intact, but the one after it, `5d3246b1163`, appended rule 84's fourth axis in place, which is an extension, and the count became 23. The checker caught it and the board did not, because a figure ages out silently while the sentence around it still reads as a finding. **Note what distinguishes this from ordinary staleness: the falsifying edit was not related to the claim, was not a correction of it, and could not have been anticipated by whoever wrote it** — every future edit to this file is a draw from the same population, so an unpinned self-referential count decays on a schedule set entirely by unrelated work. This is rule 84 turned reflexive: there the fix was to name the artifact and the unit, here it is to name the **revision**, and the fix is one hash in the prose plus the same hash in the walk that derives it. The general form is broader than git history — any statistic over "everything of kind K so far" where the writer is still producing things of kind K needs the same treatment, and the tell is that you cannot state the number without the act of stating it being in scope.

91. **Before using a column as a partition key, check the group sizes it produces against the ones the design can produce; a size the design cannot produce means the column is not the partition.** The P0.5 invocation CSVs carry both a `runId` and a `mode`, and `mode` names a phase, so keying comparison cells on `(scenario, heapFactor, mode, collector)` looks exact and reads as exact. It is not: **30 of the 699 valid rows carry `mode=latency` under a `.throughput` runId**, because a run executes both passes, so `mode` crosses runs rather than partitioning them. The pooled key produced arms of **10 and 13** where the design produces **5**, and that impossible size is the whole detection: re-keyed on `(runId, scenario, heapFactor, mode, collector)` the population is **135 arms of 5 and 8 of 3, with none of 10 or 13**. The cost of not checking is not a rounding error but a reversed conclusion. Rule 89 computes the attainable floor as `1/C(2n,n)`, so at the artifact 10-versus-10 the floor reads **5.41e-06** against the **7.22e-05** a 693-wide family needs and rule 86 comes back **achievable**, which is the exact claim rule 89 exists to refuse; at the design five-versus-five it is **3.97e-03**, **55.00x** short. A derivation that computes its own attainable range from the data inherits every keying defect in that data, so the key is checked before the range, not after.

92. **A rank can be invariant under a change of basis while the values it ranks are not, so a claim citing both must declare the basis for the values even though the rank does not need one.** P0.5 section 6.3 carried a superlative falsified by ranking `aspnet-request-load`/wks **9th of 20** arm-series by relative 1.3x-to-6.0x latency change, and that rank is **9 of 20 under all four** combinations of published-aggregate-versus-mean and pooled-versus-runId-keyed, so the falsification needs no basis declared and is as strong as a measurement over this data gets. The percentages published beside it do not share that property. `large-object-pressure`/wks is quoted at **-82.3%**, its value over means, where it ranks **3rd of 20**; over the last-invocation aggregates this document publishes everywhere else it is **+6.7%**, ranking **19th of 20** - opposite in sign and all but last in the ordering it was cited to illustrate. Two of the eight series exceeding the subject swap out in each direction between the two bases. The conclusion survives and the illustration inverts, so a reader checking the vivid number against the table above it finds a contradiction the conclusion never had.

93. **A capture group is a window, and a corrupted value can be wider than the window the pattern opened for it — which is not one failure but two, and both misdiagnose.** If the wider value still matches, the check reads the truncation and quotes it back as though it were what the text says: `([\d,]+)` over a board reading `1019.11 pairs` captures `1019`, so `1,018.5 pairs` would have passed outright. If it does not match, the check reports the *sentence* as reworded and silently retired when the sentence is intact and only the number moved — pointing the reader at the wrong artifact entirely. Both were live here, and this is the third instance of one class after negatives excluded by a `^\d+` shape test and thousands separators excluded by a bare `\d`, so the class is what gets fixed and not the instance: every numeric capture admits a decimal fraction, and every captured numeral is then expanded to the full numeral it sits inside before comparison. Expansion is asymmetric — leftward over digits and separators, rightward over digits and a following fraction but never over a comma, because `870, 92` is two figures and must not merge into one. The same root shows up in the matching direction as an unterminated literal: `0 of 69` matched four times whole-text against three terminated on the board as this was found, because a figure written later, `0 of 693`, contains the earlier one as a substring — so a check obeying rule 85 and asserting its own hit count reports `4, expected 3`, which reads as *a site was added to the board* when the board's sites are untouched. Writing this rule down moved those counts to **six and four** as of this revision, since the sentence you are reading contains both literals: the statement of the count changed the count, which is rule 90 arriving from underneath — a self-referential figure is not merely fragile against later edits, it can be falsified by the edit that records it. The general form: **a numeral has two boundaries and a check must assert both** — termination in the pattern, width in the capture — because **a check's domain is the values its text could hold, not the values its author expected to read**, and a pattern narrow enough to be readable is narrow enough to be wrong quietly.

94. **A control whose subject list is restated rather than derived cannot report “every”; it reports “every one I was told about”, and the difference is invisible in a green run.** `board-check-coverage.ps1` holds a hand-written case per check, and the moment a fifteenth check was added to `board-check.ps1` it printed **every check fired on both of its distinct payloads (29 cases)** and exited 0 with that check at zero coverage. Nothing was broken and nothing was skipped — the control simply could not see a subject it had not been handed, so its headline was true of its own list and false of its subject. This is the shape of the implementing session's F25 in a second artifact: work that never reaches the verdict, under a word that says it did. Where restating cannot be removed — a perturbation has to be written by hand for each check, unlike the sibling battery which extracts its patterns from the checker it audits — the **count** is asserted against the subject instead: the subject reports how many checks it ran, every one must own a distinct case, and a mismatch is a failure rather than a smaller number. Watched failing before it was trusted: dropping the two new cases yields `COVERAGE INCOMPLETE: board-check runs 15 check(s) but this battery declares payloads for 14`, exit 1. The general form: **a control must derive its subject from the subject, and where it cannot, it must at minimum derive the subject's size** — otherwise the next thing added to the subject is unaudited by construction, and the audit says otherwise.

95. **The basis on which a figure is published is a property of the field, not of the document, so “this document publishes basis X” is a universal over columns and has to be measured one column at a time.** A single file, `p0-5-baselines-s2.json`, carries two aggregation families with no overlap and no residue: `latencyP99Ms` is the arithmetic mean of its five invocations in **60 of 60** cells and the last invocation in **0 of 60**, and `operationsPerSecond` is a mean in **113 of 113**, while `pauseP99Ms` is the last invocation in **84 of 84**, `pauseAverageMs` in **92 of 92** and `workingSetMb` in **113 of 113**, each a mean in none. The coordinator established the last-invocation rule on the pause fields, carried it to a latency table, and reported an undeclared basis against a table whose basis was declared in the sentence directly beneath it; both halves were false and false for different reasons — one about the document, one about the field. The first attempt to measure this said **54 of 60**, which looks like a rule with six exceptions worth explaining and was instead a pool keyed without the run: rows from the throughput run also carry `mode=latency`. A near-universal with an unexplained remainder is a keying defect until proven otherwise, and the corrected key is total in both directions.

96. **A correction rewrites a sentence, so it inherits every number in that sentence: the one it came to fix and the ones it did not.** P0.5 section 6.3’s blockquote read **40 of the table’s 40 cells** are means **and 1 is the last**. The rewrite moved the cell count to **60**, which is correct and was the point of the edit, and the coincidence count to **4**, which is not: at the document’s own printed precision that count is **1** — exactly the value the correction replaced — and it is **0** exact, **5** at two decimals, **2** under “equals some invocation”, and **4** under nothing. One clause, one edit, one figure fixed and one broken, and the broken one had been right until the correction touched it.

97. **A check’s subject list is part of the check: enumerate what the tree actually holds rather than the kinds of file you had in mind, and make the check assert that extent.** P0.5’s finding-id check resolves ids cited from `*.cs`, `*.py` and `*.sh` and reports **12 cited, 12 resolved**, which reproduces exactly under its own rules. The same tree holds **6** `.ps1` scripts, they cite **4** finding ids, and one of those — `F17`, at `measure-open-loop-rates.ps1:8` — occurs **exactly once** in the whole `docs` tree and resolves to no document. The check written to catch dangling finding-id citations ships with one standing beside it, and the file type it omits is the one the data-producing run scripts are written in. This is the fourth subject-too-narrow defect in the same pair of checks, after the silent skip, the blindness to the `F<n>` form, and basename resolution, so the operational form is not “widen the list” but “derive the list and print its size”.

98. **Over a lagged channel a state report is a timestamp, not a fact: it can be true when written and false when read, so the reader must re-derive it before acting rather than blame the sender for the delay.** *This rule’s first draft said the opposite — “re-read HEAD before asserting it” — and cited the P0.5 session reporting `HEAD = 6cdeea5ba1e` while its tip was `5858cc4616e`, and quoting `132,267` collections after its own commit `750a708dde4` had corrected the figure to `132,257`.* **Both charges are false.** Measured: `git merge-base --is-ancestor 750a708dde4 6cdeea5ba1e` returns non-zero — the correction did not yet exist at the revision the message was composed at — and `1a3cffe35c0` really is four commits above PR #5, exactly as its next message said. Every state report the session sent was accurate when it left. The lag is the channel’s: replies queue, and each describes a tree that has moved by the time it arrives. The obligation is therefore the **reader’s** — re-derive from the object store, which costs one command — and the writer’s only duty is to name a hash the reader can position. The first draft got the diagnosis right in its own words (“true when written and false when read”) and then drew from it a prescription that would have changed nothing, because re-reading HEAD returns the same answer the sender already had.

99. **A count does not survive a change of population, and a counterfactual about a different population has to be recomputed rather than carried — including the part of it that flatters the other side.** Conceding the pause-variance population, the P0.5 session added that on its own n≥3 basis the coordinator’s “exactly half the cells above the median” would have been `48 of 94 = 51.06%` and so slightly wrong. Measured: at n≥3 it is **47 of 94**, which is *also* exactly 50.0%. It held the numerator fixed while moving the population, but the median moves with the population and the count above it recomputes. Rule 96 governs the numbers a correction inherits from its own sentence; this governs the numbers an argument carries into a population it is not using. Both are the same failure to re-derive, and this one is harder to see because the conclusion it supported was a concession.

100. **“Occurs” is not “is defined”: a resolution check whose predicate is occurrence passes on any mention, including a range row that defines nothing and the prose recording that nothing is defined.** P0.5’s summary table collapses nine findings into one `F13–F21` row. Measured across that tree: **F17 occurs in no markdown at all** (0 occurrences, 1 citation from `measure-open-loop-rates.ps1:8`), while **F13 occurs 8 times and is defined nowhere** — its only occurrences outside the range row are the prose documenting its absence. These are two different defects in one check and they need different fixes: F17 falls to rule 97 (widen the subject to the `.ps1` files the tree actually holds), F13 does not fall to it at all, because widening the subject cannot change a predicate. The coordinator reported F17 as a subject defect and was right about F17 and wrong that the subject was the whole of it. When a check resolves an identifier, state whether it demands a *definition* or merely a *sighting*, and make a range row fail.

101. **A band has two edges, and a counterexample confirms only the edge it arrived from: checking the near end of a range says nothing whatever about the far end.** The coordinator falsified “aspnet’s latency sits two to three orders of magnitude above the others” by finding scenarios too *close* to it, and reported the claim as holding for 6 of 9. Measured against the declared basis, the split is **3 / 3 / 3**: three scenarios nearer than 100x (`lifecycle-semantics` 8.6x, `long-lived-cache` 19.5x, `large-object-pressure` 49.6x), three inside the band, and three *beyond* 1000x (`multi-thread-throughput`, `pinning-heavy-io`, `pointer-chasing`, the last at ~3105x). It holds for **3 of 9 and fails for 6** — the falsification was correct and undercounted itself by half, because the search stopped at the end the first counterexample came from. Enumerate the whole ordering; a bound stated as a range needs both of its inequalities tested.

102. **Re-deriving a published figure, change nothing you are not forced to change — and when a subset disagrees, the identity of that subset names the change that did it.** Re-deriving P0.5’s ten scenario means the coordinator moved population *and* estimator at once: pooled raw invocations over the union of all three sessions, where the table declares the mean of six per-cell means over s2 alone. Six figures agreed and four did not — `long-lived-cache` 23.92 against **23.17**, `large-object-pressure` 10.61 against **9.10**, `allocation-churn` 3.29 against **3.46**, `low-allocation-compute` 0.43 against **0.56** — and the four are **exactly the set s3 re-ran** (set equality verified, not eyeballed), because pooling raw double-weights whichever cells a later session added five invocations to. Both defects were already on this board: rule 87 for the population, rule 95 for the basis. The recovery is the useful half: a partial disagreement is more diagnostic than a total one, so name the disagreeing set before theorising about the cause.

103. **A citation resolves to a number, not to a claim, so correcting a rule in place silently re-targets every citation of it — and an existence check is structurally unable to see that.** Walking all 107 board commits that touch `roadmap.md`, exactly **three** rule numbers have had their headline claim *replaced* rather than extended or amended: 50 and 51 at `be5bc610e00`, and 98 at `0f13853a89b`. All three still resolve, so a dangling-citation check returns clean on every one of them. The P0.5 session offered rule 50’s replacement as “a better argument for the dangling check”; it is an argument for the opposite, because rule 50 was **overwritten, not deleted**, and overwriting is precisely the case existence cannot detect. Blast radius today is zero — 0 self-citations on the board and 0 in the child’s tree at `79da938240d` for all three numbers — but that is a property of what happens to be cited, not of the practice. Since rule 22 *requires* correcting in place, this board’s numbers are mutable by design, and a citation of one must name the revision it was written against exactly as rule 14 already demands for reference locations. **Corroborated independently one round later, against this board.** The P0.5 session audited its ten distinct rule citations at board commit `2d4d196d8c7` and found one whose *number* resolved and whose *content* did not: it quoted rule 84’s operational form as “name the artifact, name the estimator, name the unit” where this board’s third clause reads “name what the integer counts” — and the compression dropped exactly what that clause was added to supply, since naming a unit still does not say which of two coincident figures the arithmetic divides. Existence was never in question: 10 of 10 resolved, 0 dangling, verified here. The defect lives in the fit between the citation and the claim it is offered for, which is why the practice that catches it is resolving the cited text and quoting it — not testing that the number exists.

104. **Search the board for a rule’s subject before adding it; a rule that exists and is not read is worth nothing, and the recurrence it was written to prevent will not announce itself.** All **three** in-place headline replacements in this board’s history are withdrawn accusations against the same child session — 3 of 3, the entire population of identity drift here. Rule 50’s corrected headline, written by me at `be5bc610e00`, says *“check the clock before charging anyone with staleness”*. Forty-eight rules later I wrote rule 98 charging that session with reporting stale state, and retracted it after running `git merge-base --is-ancestor 750a708dde4 6cdeea5ba1e` — the clock check rule 50 already prescribed, against the same session, for the same mistake. The prophylactic was in this file, under a number I had written myself, and nothing in the act of appending rule 98 required me to read it. Growth of the rule set is not the same as growth of the practice. **The same defect has a measurement form, and I committed it against this session’s own instrument.** Asked whether a reported figure of 693 well-formed pairs reproduced, I wrote a fresh ad-hoc probe, got 1106 pairs and 210 degenerate under a column set chosen on the spot, and reported that I *could not* derive 693 — recommending the figure travel as the other session’s alone rather than as reproduced. It was being derived here all along: `board-claims-check.ps1`’s `RatioDomain` computes the pair, undefined and well-formed counts over a curated `$METRIC` list of **20** columns, and two claims have been gating **870, 92 and 693** against this board on every run since before the question was asked. My ad-hoc set was wider and swept in configuration echoed into the metrics file — `heapLimitMb`, `warmupSeconds` and `steadyStateSeconds`, none of which appear in `$METRIC` — and that is the entire source of both the extra pairs and the extra degeneracy. I then argued *from* that artifact that a degeneracy predicate must be mechanical rather than a curated column list, when the curated list already in hand is precisely what avoids the problem. **A claimed non-reproduction is more corrosive than a wrong number**, because a wrong number invites a check, while a manufactured disagreement makes two agreeing instruments look disputed and invites nobody to run either. So the rule’s object generalizes from rules to derivations: **search for the derivation before writing one, and where a gated instrument already computes the quantity, that instrument is the answer — a fresh probe is at best a second opinion, and it has to say so.**

105. **Rot and narration-ahead are different defects with different fixes: rot was true and stopped being true, narration-ahead was never true.** The distinction is the P0.5 session’s, returned against an attribution I had made — I filed its F26 as the third instance of “a conclusion written ahead of its data”, and F26 records what was found, with a citation that was correct when written and became wrong when the file grew above it. This board carries an instance of the same class: rule 13’s reference moved from `src/plan/barriers.rs:317` to `:315-319` at `e02c462a27e`. Only narration-ahead is fixable by verifying before asserting; rot needs an anchor that survives movement, which is why a rot finding can legitimately ship unfixed. The count of three survives with a different member — the §6.3 Kestrel clause, which the session supplied against itself: reviewed, its citation resolved, reported “unchanged and correct” by a check that could not reach either the causal or the comparative claim.

106. **An edit’s net effect is not its intent: when an insertion moves a count by less than it added, the difference was destroyed by the insertion itself — and a tally of what you added cannot detect it.** The P0.5 session’s `79da938240d` inserted two `### F<n>` headings and the document’s heading count rose by **one**. Verified here at four revisions: `### 9.1` is present at `9f054925372` and `a46333b9b7d`, **absent** at `79da938240d` — leaving 180 lines of §9.1 hanging under `### F34` — and restored at `609009f6fdb`. Counting `###`+`####` gives 24 → 32 → 33; counting `##`+`###`+`####` gives 33 → 41 → 42. The finding holds under either basis and the constant +9 between them is exactly the nine `##` headings, so declaring the basis converted an apparent contradiction between our two counts into agreement — rule 95 earning its keep on someone else’s artifact. **The second half is why nothing caught it:** the gate at that revision touches headings in exactly one place, the `### F<n>` definition test added for rule 100, so findings headings were covered as a *by-product* of resolving citations and every other heading in the document was unowned. Coverage acquired as a side effect of a different check is coverage of that instance, not of the class. And the damage was done by the commit acting on rule 100 — which is to say by work I asked for: an insertion that satisfies the check it was written for can still destroy the artifact around it. The session’s own account adds that its first structural check fired on the correct document as well as the broken one; that is rule 88 already, run its predicate against a healthy artifact and count the false alarms, so it is cited rather than restated.

107. **A caveat that accurately bounds one claim makes the unbounded claims beside it look audited.** F27 published a collection total of `132,267` for the nine `cyclic-garbage`/wks/throughput rows that lost their pause samples, and the review of that finding said — correctly — that summing the counters double-counts, but that the `>0` versus `==0` split is monotone in the total, so the 105/25 boundary is identical under either reading. Every word of that is true and I have re-derived it from the raw per-invocation CSV rather than argued it: over the **130** blank `pauseP99Ms` rows the split is **25 / 105** under gen0-only, under gen0+gen1+gen2, under those plus induced, and under gen1+gen2, moving only to **13 / 117** under gen2-only, which is no reading of “the total”. But `132,267` is not a boundary. It is a magnitude, three sentences up, produced by precisely the sum the caveat had just named as double-counting. **Naming a defect and then reasoning about it in one direction is worse than not noticing it**, because it converts an unexamined number into an apparently examined one — and neither party challenged the magnitude afterwards. The correct figure is **132,257**: `gen0Collections` alone, which `GcTelemetry.cs:233` documents as counting every collection of generation 0 *or higher*, so the generation counters are nested and the sum adds the 10 gen1 collections a second time. I derived `132,257 / 10 / 0` over those nine rows myself. It is P0.4’s `MeanPauseMs` triple-count recurring inside a document that cites that defect. **A caveat must travel with the number it covers rather than with the finding it appears in, and naming a systematic error obliges a sweep of every figure that error touches — not an argument that one conclusion survives it.** *The reviewing sentence is quoted to me as mine and I neither claim nor disclaim it, per rule 64: my own sent messages are not in my retrievable record, `assistant_response` being far too short to hold them, so a search for the phrase returns nothing whether or not I wrote it — rule 40’s probe that cannot see its subject, caught this time before the conclusion was drawn. Rule 64 already records this session declining unverifiable authorship in the opposite direction. What is verifiable, and is the rule, is that both parties read the finding and neither corrected the magnitude.* **A second instance, mine, committed inside the message that reported the fix for the first.** I told the P0.5 session my branch stood at *seven* commits above PR #5, and attached the correct caveat — that PR #5 is not an ancestor of this branch, so the figure is a set difference and not a distance. The caveat was right. The number was wrong under **every** reading: the distance from the shared base `df9c6988c20` to `dc01449ffc1` is **126**, and this session’s own segment through that same commit is **6**. Seven is neither, and both of those *are* genuine distances — the ancestor test passes for each — so there is no frame in which seven was the answer. **Naming the frame is not measuring the quantity**, and a magnitude that arrives wearing a correct epistemic qualifier is harder to audit than a bare one, because the qualifier is where a reader’s scepticism gets spent: mine drew attention to the reference and away from the arithmetic. The durable form pins both ends — `df9c6988c20..dc01449ffc1` is stable forever where `..HEAD` re-rots on the next commit — which is the both-ends discipline the rot rule already prescribes for citations, applied to a count.

108. **A zero-width interval has at least four causes and only one is the defect the detector is hunting; the discriminator is whether more data dissolves it.** This corrects the shape of the degeneracy check proposed for P0.6, which would “compute universally” and flag every constant cell. Measured over the P0.5 invocation CSVs with cells keyed on (scenario, collector, mode, heapFactor) — **113 cells**, s2 595 rows, union 699 — **five** columns are degenerate in **113 of 113** cells and not one of them is a finding. `heapFactor` is degenerate **because it is a member of the cell key**: grouping by a variable makes it constant inside every group, so a detector applied to partitioned data necessarily fires on its own partition, and it fires hardest on the variable the analysis is *about*. `heapLimitMb`, `warmupSeconds` and `steadyStateSeconds` are configuration echoed into the metrics file. And `inducedCollections` is the case curation cannot reach — a **genuine measurement**, neither a knob nor a key member, constant at zero in every cell because nothing induced a collection. An exclusion list built by asking “is this a knob?” keeps it, and it fires anyway. **The discriminator is the implementer's own monotonicity lemma turned into an instrument.** Adding invocations to a cell can break a constant vector and can never create one, so degeneracy is non-increasing under more data — therefore the degeneracy that *survives* more data is structural, and the degeneracy that *dissolves* was undersampling. Exactly **16** cells gained invocations between s2 and the union, touching exactly the four scenarios s3 re-ran, and exactly **four** columns moved: `arrivalRatePerSecond` 54→48, `gen1Collections` 60→57, `gen0Collections` 48→45, `gen2Collections` 83→82, totals 830→817. Those four are the true positives; the five that did not move are structural. So the predicate is not “is this column constant” but **“is this column constant *and* does it stay constant when the cell grows”** — mechanical, needing no curated list, and classifying the grouping key correctly for free. **A check that reports a true statement about the partition rather than about the data is not a false positive; it is a correct answer to a question nobody asked, which is harder to notice and much harder to argue with.**

109. **Write for the person who has to decide, not for the person who did the work: a report that needs a glossary has not reported anything.** The user read PR #5 and could not parse *resolution floor*, *half-width*, *heap factor*, *throughput ratio*, *blind band*, *cell*, *invocation* or *minimum-heap calibration* — **8** unexplained terms in one description, none of them defined in it. Each has a plain equivalent that costs nothing: the smallest speed difference this machine can detect; how far the measured range reaches either side of the middle; how much memory the program got, as a multiple of the least it can survive on; one collector’s speed divided by the other’s; the range of noise levels no alarm covers; one program at one memory size under one collector; a single run of a program; and measuring that survival minimum. **No precision is lost in the translation, and that is the test** — if the plain sentence is exactly as exact, the jargon was never carrying the precision, only the membership. **Jargon also hides errors — including the one I made about the jargon.** That same description contained *fine-arm*, and I reported it as denoting nothing after searching the write-up, finding **0** occurrences, and stating that result over the whole project. It denotes something exact: control 7 injects two deliberate slowdowns, a coarse one near 16.7% and a fine one near 2%, and the fine arm is the one whose measurement precision the noise alarm bounds. At `9f054925372` the term appears **6** times across **5** files — harness source, raw control output, machine notes — and **0** times in the document that used it. **So the true defect is narrower and worse than the one I published: the write-up borrowed a term that lives only in the source code**, where no reader of the write-up would ever meet it, and being real made it *less* visible rather than more. My own error was a search scoped to one file with its conclusion stated over the project — the scope error this board has already recorded twice against others and once against me, arriving a third time inside a rule about clarity. A reader fluent in the dialect skims past an undefined term; a reader who is not cannot challenge it; and I could not tell a real term from an invented one without a search I had not run. The failure mode is the one this board keeps recording in numbers — an unexamined token that looks audited because of the company it keeps. So: **anything the user reads — PR descriptions, issue bodies, reports in chat — uses ordinary words, defines at first use any term it genuinely cannot avoid, and gives magnitudes with their units and their direction** (“about 19x slower”, not “0.052”). Precision on this board stays as it is, because a term defined here is a term defined; what is forbidden is a term defined nowhere.

110. **Keep upstream work and LXR integration on different branches.** In `kkokosa/runtime`, `main` mirrors `upstream/main`; the long-lived `lxr` branch contains the complete LXR roadmap history. Every Implement action creates its child session with `base_branch="lxr"`, every LXR step branch starts from the exact current `lxr` tip, and every LXR pull request targets `lxr` rather than `main`. Never fall back to the project default when `lxr` is absent or stale: stop, show the two hashes, and repair the integration branch first. Push the verified step hash explicitly, then compare the pull request merge base with the recorded `lxr` dependency tip. Unrelated runtime or GC work starts from `main` or `upstream/main` and does not inherit LXR changes.

## P0 — Parity contract, reference oracle, and measurement baseline
- **Status:** planned
- **Summary:** Establish what parity means before writing any collector code: build both candidate oracles, extract the paper's real acceptance targets, enumerate every mechanism to be ported, and capture honest built-in GC baselines.

### P0.1 — Pin and build both reference revisions

- **Status:** done
- **Summary:** Both oracle pairs built under WSL2 and verified genuinely LXR by runtime banner rather than exit code; HEAD is fully observable, PLDI is not, and the mechanism-organized diff with per-mechanism oracle recommendations and coupled sets is delivered in `docs/design/lxr-port/`.
- **Correctness:** HEAD `(0682434, 304ce69d)` passes 96/96 release runs with zero crashes or panics; PLDI `(abbdd1d, df8d30a3)` **fails outright** at 3/8 and 5/8 single-iteration and 1/8 and 2/8 sustained, tripping its own barrier assertion `assert!(old.is_null() || rc::count(old) != 0, "zero rc count")` at `plan/barriers.rs:315-319` (condition at `:316`) in `FieldLoggingBarrier::slow` — a field overwrite whose old target already has RC zero, gated by `cfg(any(sanity, debug_assertions))`, which is why release SIGSEGVs on the same corrupt state instead of panicking. The instability is **not** explained by revision skew: a differential run at core `4d4e516c` agreed with the pin in all 24 antlr/`-n 5` cells and produced the same pass set, disproving the hypothesis that the pin's `Fix stw LXR` commits were the difference. **Corrected in P0.3:** HEAD's clean runs are not evidence that the RC invariant holds there, because at `304ce69d` no barrier-side check exists at all — the only `zero rc count` assertion is in `util/sanity/sanity_checker.rs:311-316` (condition at `:312`) behind `cfg(feature = "sanity")`, which is not a default feature and was not enabled by the build recipe, so it was compiled out. The comparison was never run.
- **Benchmarks:** Reference-only numbers, no .NET comparison; recorded per configuration with invocation counts and every failure listed. Anomaly carried to P0.3 and closed there: hsqldb p99 of 0.34-0.40 ms on PLDI versus 54-56 ms on HEAD like-for-like at `-n 5` and 2000 MB, two orders of magnitude on the metric LXR exists for, from one benchmark on a noisy host, traced by P0.3 probe 2 to induced-collection policy rather than any LXR mechanism.
- **Dependencies:** none
- **References:** `docs/design/lxr-port/`; oracle pairs (`abbdd1d`, `df8d30a3`) and (`0682434`, `304ce69d`); secondary builds at core `4d4e516c` and `9625c174`, behaviorally indistinguishable; `plan/barriers.rs:315-319`; `src/args.rs` `LAZY_MU_REUSE_BLOCK_SWEEPING`

### P0.2 — Extract paper acceptance targets from the PDF

- **Status:** done
- **Summary:** Targets extracted and independently re-verified against the local PDF; the paper is the arXiv Extended Version of 1 Nov 2022, not the PLDI proceedings, so citations name arXiv table and page numbers and proceedings numbering is not assumed to match.
- **Correctness:** Every quoted number cites a table or figure in the local PDF, cross-read four ways including a rendered-page check, with the coordinator independently confirming Tables 1, 5, 6 and 7 from the pixels; two errata were found in the paper itself, Table 7's `!Lazy%` summary rows printing a minimum of 22 above a maximum of 2 against a true range of 0 to 22, and a 90th-percentile column that section 4 promises "in tabular form" but Table 4 does not contain.
- **Benchmarks:** Verified targets are throughput geomean `0.958` versus G1 at 2x heap, LXR-only pause p50/p95 of `5.0`/`7.5` ms mean and `3.0`/`4.7` ms geomean, reclamation split `94.3`/`0.6`/`5.1` from the mean row, and barrier overhead `1.016` geomean measured against a no-barrier full-heap Immix build rather than against G1.
- **Dependencies:** P0.1
- **References:** `C:\github\lxr-reference\paper\2210.17175.pdf`; `docs/design/lxr-port/P0.2-paper-targets.md`; Tables 1, 4, 5, 6, 7

### P0.3 — Build the mechanism parity ledger

- **Status:** done
- **Summary:** Delivered 26 rows across seven groups, each declaring its oracle, provenance tag, .NET realization and closure evidence, merged as PR #3 (squash `8a63e85178b`). Two findings changed the plan: LXR declares pinning unsupported, so row R05 has declared oracle `none` and must be closed port-side; and induced GC is serviced at HEAD rather than ignored, the earlier claim having rested on citations behind a non-default feature.
- **Correctness:** `scripts/verify-ledger.sh` run with no argument against a `git archive` extract of the merge commit `8a63e85178b`, outside any repository: 127 citations resolved, 50/50 byte-identical against the read-only reference, 11 flagged / 11 acknowledged / 0 unacknowledged, 26 index rows / 26 detail blocks matching §4's self-reported total, one declared oracle per coupled group, `C06 -> R05` redirect intact, 0 trailing whitespace, exit 0, byte-identical across two runs. The gate rejects citations to code that is not compiled, self-locates to the tree it ships in, and ships `verify-gate.sh` as its own positive control requiring PASS / FAIL / PASS on a copy differing by exactly one row.
- **Benchmarks:** None directly; the ledger defines which mechanisms later benchmark deltas must be attributable to. It also closed P0.1's hsqldb p99 anomaly (PLDI 0.34-0.40 ms versus HEAD 54-56 ms) rather than carrying it: probe 2 proved the cause is induced-collection policy and not an LXR mechanism difference, since hsqldb's `MemoryWatcherThread` calls `System.gc()`, HEAD services it as a full stop-the-world collection, and PLDI cannot because the body of `handle_user_collection_request` is commented out.
- **Dependencies:** P0.1, P0.2
- **References:** `docs/design/lxr-port/P0.1-mechanism-diff.md`; paper §2-§3; head `mmtk-core/src/plan/lxr/*` versus the PLDI `lxr` feature closure over `src/policy/immix/*`, `src/util/rc.rs`, `src/util/cm.rs`; `mmtk-openjdk/openjdk/barriers/*`

### P0.4 — Build the benchmark harness and scenario matrix

- **Status:** done
- **Summary:** Harness landed on `main` as squash merge `f6e93305259` (PR #4, 48 files, +10,994), covering all ten scenarios with a runner, worker, control suite, verification gate and gate-of-the-gate. No runtime, EE or JIT change proved necessary: effective GC configuration reads back through `GetConfigurationVariables`, tiering and PGO through `TieredCompilationSettings`, the future collector arm through `GCName`/`GCPath`, and bounded dumps through `DbgEnableMiniDump`.
- **Correctness:** Verified at the merge commit rather than at the attested tip, because the squash means `f5f1c6ed8b3` is not an ancestor of `main` and no attested hash carries. Tree identity was checked instead and holds across the whole repository, not just the harness path — the tree hashes of the attested tip and `f6e93305259` are equal, so the squash neither dropped nor swept in anything. The gate was then run from a `git archive` extract of `f6e93305259` outside any worktree: `PASS` with a full smoke results set, `exit 2` and **zero** `RESULT: PASS` lines when results are absent, `exit 2` on an empty results directory, `exit 3` and `DEGRADED` under `--no-results`, and `exit 1` naming the gap when pointed at a partial two-of-ten-scenario run. Two High review findings were fixed and regression-tested: `MeanPauseMs` triple-counted collections because `GC.CollectionCount(0)` counts gen0-or-higher, reporting 1.9306 ms against a true 3.9578 ms with a factor that varies by generation mix and so does not cancel between arms; and the bootstrap interval was zero-width at n=1, which made any ratio other than exactly 1.0 read as significant on the default smoke path.
- **Benchmarks:** No collector comparison is published here — this step builds and proves the instrument, and P0.5 measures with it. The measurement result that does bind later steps is negative: control 7 could not reliably resolve a 2% injected effect on this host, reaching the 1.6% target at n=8, at n=15, and not at all across three runs of the same binary, with direct paired probes returning 1.0221, 0.9649 and 0.9922 — a 2% signal under a ±3% single-invocation spread with the sign flipping. That is the paper's 1.6%-inside-noise problem reproduced locally. The assertion was therefore split: a coarse ~16.7% injection is asserted, a null replicate guards against manufactured effects, and the barrier-scale arm is measured and published without gating the verdict.
- **Evidence:** Run artifacts are gitignored and lived only in the child worktree, so 919 files (10.36 MB) covering `runs/`, `smoke/` and `probe/` were copied to session state before that worktree was removed, verified byte-identical by SHA256 with a negative control proving the comparison can detect a difference. Crash dumps were excluded as regenerable bulk. Without this the numbers quoted in §8 of the design document would have had no surviving source.
- **Dependencies:** none
- **References:** paper §4 methodology

### P0.5 — Measure Workstation and Server GC baselines

- **Status:** done
- **Summary:** Speed and pause measurements for both of .NET's existing collectors, across all ten test programs, at three memory sizes each, published together with the raw numbers so anyone can recompute every figure. The step delivered what it was asked for. What it found is that this machine cannot support the target we set: the same test on the same machine gives different absolute numbers on different days, so from here on we compare the two collectors against each other within a single run, never across runs. Merged as `d272dabb7b4`.
- **Correctness:** Tested, and **the test failed** — which is the most useful thing this step produced. Each test program was run twice, on separate days. Of 16 re-measured combinations, 12 disagreed by more than both their own run-to-run scatter and the smallest difference this machine can reliably detect (about 8%). Typical gap 14.5%, worst 89.6%. Broken down rather than averaged: 6 of them were not comparable at all, because a defect meant they were fed different amounts of work; of the 10 genuinely comparable ones, 7 still disagreed. All 8 speed comparisons moved in the same direction, which happens by chance about 1 time in 256, and they tracked how busy the machine was — 12.73% busy on one day against 16.41% on the other. The scatter was written down rather than averaged away, so the method survived even though the claim did not.
- **Benchmarks:** Existing collectors only — Workstation and Server. No LXR numbers exist yet and none are claimed. Checked through the live board: 3 result sets, 144 collector fields, none mentioning LXR, none recorded while the machine was overloaded. Within a single run the two collectors can be compared; across runs they cannot. Server is faster than Workstation on some programs and much slower on others, and which one wins flips depending on how much memory the program is given, so no single winner can be stated.
- **Evidence:** PR #5, merged 13 Aug as `d272dabb7b4`; 57 files, all under `docs/design/lxr-port/`. The merge squashed `9f054925372`, and the two carry an identical file tree (`715c65fd9d6`), so every line number cited against the branch still resolves against `main`. Checked from a `git archive` extract outside any working copy, so nothing uncommitted could contribute.

### P0.6 — Resolve the baseline anomalies and fix the measurement methodology

- **Status:** failed
- **Summary:** The measurement repair was completed and committed locally at `857125d412b`, but P0.6 failed three of its five acceptance criteria. It repaired lifecycle calibration and the pinning-throughput test. It did not explain the large-object reversal, establish the required noise margin, or find a sufficiently stable latency measure. No LXR benchmark was run.
- **Correctness:** **Two pass, three fail.** Lifecycle calibration now tests every planned memory size instead of assuming that more memory always helps; it selected 68, 104, and 312 MiB only after both collectors passed twice at each size. The pinning test now disables simulated I/O for throughput comparisons, because enabled I/O made both collectors look equal. The large-object reversal reproduced — Server was about 1.12x faster at 88 MiB and about 9.64x slower at 134 MiB — but its cause remains unknown. Changing Server heap count and removing large objects explained only part of the loss; pinning made all 10 attempts run out of memory.
- **Benchmarks:** 751 fresh processes were attempted and 707 produced valid reports. The 60-second noise test still left about 1.35% uncertainty on either side, missing the predeclared 1.25% target, so the intended safety margin cannot be claimed on this machine. With up to 15 runs, typical variation was 2.13% for p50 latency, 11.57% for p95, and 14.59% for p99; p99 with five runs is rejected. The committed evidence passed 24 of 24 clean-copy and deliberately-broken-input checks; the harness built with 0 warnings and 0 errors and passed 66 of 66 tests.
